items.example: Designing a sticker of a country or a landmark? Start from the crowd-drawn outline, not the GIS-accurate border. The wobbly, over-rounded version is what a viewer's eye accepts in half a second; the accurate one reads as slightly off to everyone who never looked at a survey map.
items.plain: Ask a thousand people to draw a shape from memory and their average drawing is not the true shape; it is a simpler, rounder version. That averaged mistake is the picture people actually store in their heads. If you design for recognition, match the remembered shape, like drawing a heart the way it looks on a Valentine instead of in a biology book.

questions.q: What does the composite crowd map reveal about memory?
questions.a: People's mental maps are distorted in shared, systematic ways; the average sketch shows the common distortion, not the true border.

questions.q: Why is the shared distortion useful to a designer?
questions.a: Recognition runs on the mental model, so matching the remembered shape reads faster and more correct to viewers than matching reality.

items.headline: Hitman's Bodies Fell So Well Because the Physics Cheated
items.deck: A 2001 paper from IO Interactive powered gaming's first famous ragdolls by deleting velocity from the simulation. Believable beats accurate.
items.lead: In 2001, IO Interactive's Thomas Jakobsen published 'Advanced Character Physics', the method behind Hitman: Codename 47's cloth, plants and ragdoll deaths that the press oxymoronically praised as 'lifelike death animations'. The core move is outrageous: throw velocity out of the simulation and keep only positions.
ptrs: Verlet integration, borrowed from molecular dynamics, stores just each particle's current and previous position; velocity is implied by the difference, so position and velocity can never drift out of sync, the classic source of exploding game physics.

The update is one line: next = current + (current - previous) + acceleration. Dropping the hidden factor from 2 to 1.99 adds free drag. It is fast and stable, not perfectly accurate; energy can leak, and on screen nobody cares.

Collisions and sticks are solved by relaxation: nudge the particles to satisfy each rule, repeat a few times, and the system settles. A rigid body becomes a handful of particles joined by stick constraints.
Jakobsen even included a square-root approximation for extra speed, because the goal was never simulation truth; it was a corpse that crumpled convincingly against furniture.
The screen-design lesson: believability is a look, not a solver. Audiences read weight, looseness and consequence, not equations.
items.why: This is the most buildable physics idea you will ever meet: a rope or cloth sim is about twenty lines of Python, no math beyond subtraction. It also rewires how you watch games: every slick cape and collapsing enemy is probably this 2001 trick wearing a new suit.

The core move is outrageous: throw velocity out of the simulation and keep only positions. Verlet integration, borrowed from molecular dynamics, stores just each particle's current and previous position; velocity is implied by the difference, so position and velocity can never drift out of sync, the classic source of exploding game physics. The update is one line: next = current + (current - previous) + acceleration. Dropping the hidden factor from 2 to 1.99 adds free drag. It is fast and stable, not perfectly accurate; energy can leak, and on screen nobody cares. Collisions and sticks are solved by relaxation: nudge the particles to satisfy each rule, repeat a few times, and the system settles. A rigid body becomes a handful of particles joined by stick constraints. Jakobsen even included a square-root approximation for extra speed, because the goal was never simulation truth; it was a corpse that crumpled convincingly against furniture. The screen-design lesson: believability is a look, not a solver. Audiences read weight, looseness and consequence, not equations.
items.example: Build a rope tonight: ten points in a list, each with a current and previous position. Every frame, apply the one-line Verlet update with gravity, pin the top point, then run five relaxation passes pulling neighboring points back to their rest distance. You get a swinging, drapeable chain, the same skeleton Hitman used for bodies and capes.
items.plain: Normal physics tracks where things are and how fast they move, and the two can disagree and explode. This trick only remembers where each point is now and where it was a moment ago; speed is just the difference, like knowing you walked forward because of where your feet were. Then you nudge points until rules like 'these two stay one stick apart' hold. It is fake, and it looks completely real.

questions.q: What does Verlet integration store instead of velocity?
questions.a: Each particle's current and previous position; velocity is implied by the difference between them.

questions.q: How are constraints like sticks enforced?
questions.a: By relaxation: move particles to satisfy each rule, repeat a few iterations, and the system settles.

questions.q: Why did Jakobsen accept an inaccurate method?
questions.a: Games need fast, stable, believable motion, not true physics; small energy leaks are invisible on screen.

items.headline: GLM-5.4 Thinks in Circles and Punches at 2T
items.deck: Z.ai's new flagship loops 28 shared layers twice instead of growing. The claim: 750B parameters behaving like 2T-3T.
items.lead: Z.ai released GLM-5.4 on November 23, its first flagship built on a Loop Transformer: a shared block of 28 layers runs twice per token, and the lab claims intelligence comparable to 2T-3T parameter models at a 750B scale. The bet is that reasoning needs more compute per token, not more memorized weights.
ptrs: The loop idea dates to the 2018 Universal Transformer, but looped models trained from scratch lagged behind. Z.ai instead converted an already pre-trained GLM-5 base into a looper through continued training, about 10% extra compute in their controlled 30B comparison, where the looped twin clearly won at equal parameter count.

Three tricks keep looping stable at 750B: per-token gated updates so each pass writes a controlled amount into the residual stream (first pass builds context, second refines), a hybrid KV cache that reuses the first pass's sparse KV and adds only a sliding window, and reuse of the first pass's attention indices at zero extra indexing cost.
The architecture was validated progressively at 1B, 4B, 30B and 750B before the flagship commitment; at 1M token context, the lab says deployment cost stays controlled.
Known limitation, in their words: 'marathon thinking', the model gets caught in overly long reasoning loops, though the extended self-correction keeps improving accuracy.

Availability: live on chat.z.ai now, API coming soon, open weights promised after safety hardening. Z.ai frames the release as the start of 'generalized coding', code as the foundation for tasks far beyond programming.
HN discussion (small thread): commenters flagged looping as one of the few known levers for more reasoning without a bigger hardware budget, and asked how adaptive loop counts might work.
items.why: If looping keeps delivering, the future of strong models is smaller weights run longer, which is exactly the direction that puts serious models within reach of hardware like yours. Watch whether open weights land; a 750B looper needs a datacenter, but the trick scales down.

The architecture was validated progressively at 1B, 4B, 30B and 750B before the flagship commitment, and at 1M token context the lab says deployment cost stays controlled. GLM-5.4 is live on chat.z.ai now, an API is coming soon, and open weights are promised after safety hardening; Z.ai frames the release as the start of 'generalized coding', code as the foundation for tasks far beyond programming.
items.example: Think of debugging. A standard model reads your broken code once and answers. A looped model is closer to reading the code, forming a hunch, then reading it again with the hunch in mind before answering, same brain, second pass. That re-read is where the claimed reasoning jump comes from.
items.plain: Bigger AI models are mostly bigger memory: more stored facts. But hard problems need more thinking, not more memory. This model reuses the same block of layers twice per word, like reading a tough chapter a second time instead of buying a second textbook. It thinks deeper without getting bigger, at the cost of taking longer, sometimes much longer, which Z.ai admits is still a problem.

questions.q: What is a Loop Transformer?
questions.a: A model where a weight-shared block of layers runs multiple iterations per token, deepening reasoning without adding parameters.

questions.q: How did Z.ai avoid the instability of looping at 750B scale?
questions.a: Per-token gated updates between passes, a hybrid KV cache (shared sparse KV plus a sliding window), and reusing the first pass's attention indices.

questions.q: What is 'marathon thinking'?
questions.a: GLM-5.4's admitted tendency to get caught in overly long reasoning loops, which improves accuracy but costs time.

items.headline: Tonight You Are the Program Director
items.deck: Spelunkr streams the Internet Archive's forgotten videos as 37 live channels. Watch one block like a producer, then program your own.
items.lead: Spelunkr is a free, always-live TV network built entirely from the Internet Archive's forgotten videos: 37 channels and counting, 4,395 hours, all running 24/7 like real broadcast. Tonight's exercise is not to watch TV; it is to steal how a channel is programmed.
ptrs: Open spelunkr.tv in any browser, press any key, and you get a cable-style guide: Saturday Morning Rewind, Computer Chronicles, Late Nite Local, Unpaid Programming and more, synced live around the clock.
Pick ONE channel and watch a full block. Take notes like a program director: what opens the block, what follows, how long each piece runs, where the mood shifts.
The craft insight: a channel is a playlist with intent. Order creates meaning; a 45-minute oddity lands completely differently after a five-minute cartoon.

Now apply it: program a 30-minute 'channel' out of your own TechBlast reels, opening hook, middle depth, strong closer, and publish it as a playlist. That ordering work is the actual television craft, and it is free to practice.
Cost check: free, no install, no account wall on the guide, works on your Windows PC and your phone; all source material comes from the Internet Archive's public collection.
items.why: You batch-make reels; programming is the layer above making. One evening of studying how Spelunkr sequences dead TV into a channel you cannot stop watching teaches you more about retention than ten editing tutorials. Challenge accepted, one block, notes on your phone.

items.example: Watch one hour of the Computer Chronicles channel with a notes app. Write down the runtime of each segment and one word for its mood. You will end up with a block template, for example short-quirky, long-deep, medium-uptempo, that you can copy directly onto your next reel playlist.
items.plain: Old TV channels never let you pick episodes; someone arranged shows in an order that kept you watching. This website rebuilds that experience for free from archived videos. By watching one block and writing down the order and length of each piece, you learn the scheduling trick, then you can arrange your own videos the same way.

items.headline: One number OpenAI says predicts the future - learn to read it
items.deck: While everyone argues about benchmark scores, OpenAI's chief scientist just published the metric his lab actually steers by: perplexity. GPT-3.5 sat at 0.99, GPT-4 at 0.91 - and at 0.76 the math breakthroughs started. Here is how to read the ladder.
items.lead: Jakub Pachocki, OpenAI's chief scientist, published 'Perplexity and Intelligence' on November 22 with an unusually concrete disclosure: the internal log-perplexity numbers his lab uses to track pretraining progress. His argument - capabilities emerge predictably as this one number falls, so the industry should adopt it as a shared metric and tie safety limits to it.
items.body: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on held-out data; lower means better predictions, and it is equivalent to the cross-entropy loss you see in training logs. Pachocki's post is built on a claim OpenAI rarely makes this explicitly: that modern AI capability is mostly one dial - training a better compressor - and that this dial's reading has predicted each capability leap. His disclosed ladder, on OpenAI's main internal eval set: GPT-3.5 sat at log-perplexity about 0.99 and could hold fluent conversation; GPT-4 at about 0.91 could use chain-of-thought productively; current models are below 0.8; and when a model hit about 0.76, it 'started producing groundbreaking results' on open math problems, delivered in a single Slack thread. He expects the next transformative window around 0.68-0.7, without claiming to know what those capabilities will be. The policy ask is the point: he proposes perplexity as a shared cross-lab metric with common limits developers commit not to cross until monitoring catches up - for example, a successor to chain-of-thought monitors. He is equally upfront about the metric's four weaknesses: labs evaluate on different datasets, perplexity maps to no single task, chain-of-thought reasoning boosts capability without lowering perplexity, and the achievable floor is unknown - and near the floor, small gains mean big leaps. Publishing internal numbers, he says, costs OpenAI competitive secrecy but buys a shared scientific basis for pacing. The Hacker News discussion ran to 482 points.
ptrs: Perplexity = how surprised the model is by the next token, averaged over held-out data. Lower is better. Log-perplexity is the same number as cross-entropy loss - the exact value in your training logs.
OpenAI's disclosed ladder (internal eval set): GPT-3.5 about 0.99 (fluent chat), GPT-4 about 0.91 (productive chain-of-thought), today's models below 0.8, math breakthroughs starting at about 0.76.
Next predicted window: 0.68-0.7 log-perplexity, capabilities unknown - his point is that capabilities EMERGE at thresholds; nobody pre-orders them.
The proposal: make perplexity a shared industry metric, and set common development limits tied to it that labs do not cross until monitoring (like a successor to CoT monitors) catches up.

Four honest weaknesses he lists: datasets differ across labs, the metric maps to no real task, chain-of-thought gains don't show in perplexity, and the floor is unknown - near it, tiny drops hide huge jumps.
Why it cost OpenAI something: publishing internal perplexity tells competitors exactly where they stand; the post says safety transparency outweighed that.
HN discussion hit 482 points - community reaction, not a verified endorsement.
items.why: You are training to be an AI engineer, and this is the field's master gauge explained by the person holding it. When the next model launches with cherry-picked benchmark wins, you will have a better question to ask: what is the loss, on what held-out set, and where does that sit on the ladder? That one habit makes you un-hypeable.
items.example: Next model announcement you see, run the Pachocki test: ignore the demo, look for any disclosed perplexity or loss on a held-out set, and place it on the ladder - near 0.9 is GPT-4-class, below 0.8 is current frontier, 0.68-0.7 is the window OpenAI itself says to watch. No number disclosed? That silence is also data.

questions.q: Does lower perplexity mean the model is right more often?
questions.a: Not directly - it means the model predicts held-out text better on average. Pachocki's own caveat: perplexity maps to no single task, and chain-of-thought reasoning makes models far more capable without lowering perplexity at all. It tracks the substrate, not any one skill.

questions.q: Why would a lab want a shared metric it also warns is flawed?
questions.a: Because pacing needs any ruler all labs can read the same way. His argument: perplexity is the one metric that has predicted capability emergence for years, so despite four known weaknesses it is the best candidate for common limits tied to monitoring milestones.

questions.q: What happens near the 'floor'?
questions.a: Real text has inherent randomness, so loss can never reach zero - and nobody knows the floor's exact value. As models approach it, the same 0.01 drop corresponds to a bigger capability jump, which is why the 0.68-0.7 window matters even though it looks like a small step.

items.plain: AI labs grade their models by how well they guess the next word in fresh text - one number called perplexity. OpenAI's chief scientist just published their scores: every big ability showed up when that number dropped past a mark. He wants every lab to share this number and agree on speed limits.
items.image_alt: Cut-paper bar chart: four bars descending left to right - tall cobalt, slightly shorter vermilion, shorter amber, shortest cobalt
items.image_caption: Left to right, log-perplexity: GPT-3.5 ~0.99 - GPT-4 ~0.91 - math breakthroughs ~0.76 - next window ~0.69. Lower bar, stronger model.

items.headline: Color and type share one volume knob - pick who shouts
items.deck: A loud palette plus an expressive typeface is not double the energy - it is visual static. Type foundry Timeless Type's latest note explains why the eye gives color and letterforms one shared attention budget, and how to decide which one carries the accent.
items.lead: A new essay from the Timeless Type studio lays out a rule most beginners learn the hard way: color and typography draw from the same pool of viewer attention, so when both shout at once, neither is heard. The fix is a deliberate casting decision - one disruptor per design, the other element playing support.
items.body: The essay's core claim is physiological: the eye does not process 'chromatic vibrance' and 'letterform silhouette' in separate departments - it measures total disruption against the background. So a highly decorative display face (extreme stroke contrast, swashes, wild counters) already consumes the entire attentional budget; flood it with neon color or gradients and edge recognition collapses into 'chromatic noise'. The inverse also holds: when the brand demands safety orange or acid yellow, the type must be structurally calm - disciplined grotesques and austere geometrics survive chromatic violence because their clean edges anchor the composition. Why it fails: saturated color creates simultaneous contrast that makes edges shimmer, while intricate letterforms live and die by edge definition - the two mechanisms fight on the same turf. The usual patches (drop shadows, white outlines, framing blocks) only add clutter over a foundational imbalance. The studio's diagnostics are concrete: strip the layout to black and white - if the type is expressive without pigment, keep color understated; test the palette at full saturation over neutral letterforms - if the palette alone carries the energy, keep the type modest; check edges at small mobile sizes; reserve gradients for plain type only; and write into the brand document which element - type or color - is the official disruptor across packaging, billboards and UI.
ptrs: The shared-budget rule: the eye measures total visual disruption, not color and type separately - both draw from one attentional pool.
Expressive type (swashes, extreme contrast, wild counters) + loud color = collapsed edges and sensory exhaustion. Pick one.
Loud palette + neutral type works: clean grotesques and rigid geometrics anchor against saturated fields.
Why it fails: saturated color makes edges shimmer (simultaneous contrast); complex glyphs need crisp edges to be read. Same turf, direct conflict.
Drop shadows and outline patches treat the symptom - the real fix is rebalancing which element shouts.
Five diagnostics: the black-and-white strip test, max-saturation-over-neutral-type test, small-screen edge check, gradients only on plain type, and a written brand rule naming the disruptor.
items.why: Your reels and thumbnails live or die on exactly this: a flashy font on a saturated background reads as mush on a phone screen. One casting decision - is the TYPE the star or is the COLOR the star - instantly makes your graphics look intentional instead of assembled.
items.example: Take your next thumbnail: if you want that wild display font, set it in ink or white on a flat muted background and let the letterforms perform. If you want a screaming vermilion background, switch the font to a plain bold grotesque and let the color carry it. Then shrink the design to phone size - if the glyph edges dissolve, you have your answer.

questions.q: Why can't a strong palette and a fancy typeface both be 'the accent'?
questions.a: The eye evaluates total disruption against the background through one optical channel - it does not budget attention separately for hue and silhouette. Two maximal signals compete for the same budget, and the glyph edges lose.

questions.q: What is the black-and-white test for?
questions.a: Strip the layout to pure black and white. If the typography feels expressive and complete without pigment, the letterforms are already the event - so the color you add later should stay quiet. It reveals which element is doing the work before you commit.

items.plain: Your eyes treat loud colors and fancy letters as noise from the same speaker. If both are at full volume, you hear static. Good designers let one shout and the other whisper - like a bright red poster with plain type, or a gorgeous font in simple black.
items.image_alt: Two posters side by side: one ornate ink letterform on plain white, one small calm cobalt circle on a loud vermilion field
items.info_alt: Diagram: a balance scale weighing an ornate shape against a solid circle, one side up one down, with two sliders below set high and low
items.info_caption: One budget, two claimants. Ornate type up means color down; saturated color up means type down. Balance is a decision, not an accident.

items.headline: GTA 6's secret weapon is a field guide
items.deck: The loudest game launch in history - $1.8 billion on day one - ships with 60 collectible bird species, and Audubon sent an actual birder to find them all. His verdict: the wildlife is placed like a real ecosystem, and that is why the world feels alive.
items.lead: Grand Theft Auto VI launched November 19 to $1.8 billion in first-day revenue, and among its collectible systems - 338 vehicles, 205 weapons - sits a stranger one: at least 60 bird species you can study through in-game binoculars. Audubon magazine's Nicholas Lund tracked down every one, and his field report is a masterclass in how believable worlds are built.
items.body: Lund's review, published November 20 in Audubon, reads like a real birding trip log. The mechanics are simple: look at any bird through your binoculars, hold a button to 'study' it, and it enters your Progress menu. The design lesson is in the placement. The map respects the real ecological boundaries of South Florida: herons, gulls and other waterbirds concentrate in the southern coasts, Red-bellied Woodpeckers and Wood Storks appear farther north, owls come out at night, and actual introduced Florida exotics - Monk Parakeets, Spot-breasted Orioles, Red Junglefowl - show up exactly where a Florida birder would expect them. Lund's advice to players is the same as real birding: stop chasing species lists, find the habitat, and the species follow. The inaccuracies are just as instructive: critically endangered Whooping Cranes are weirdly common, Golden Eagles soar over mountains Florida does not have, and a few species are renamed because Carolina and Baltimore do not exist in the GTA universe - consistency with the fiction beats accuracy to our world. And the deepest accuracy is not the birds at all but the landscape: mangrove beaches, grassy swamps, roadkill on highways, the fonts on roadside fruit stands. Pre-release marketing promised 62 species; the official screen lists 60. The result: players are pausing mid-crime-spree to birdwatch, because the world rewards attention the way a real place does.
ptrs: GTA 6 launched November 19 with $1.8 billion day-one revenue; its Progress menu tracks 338 vehicles, 205 weapons - and 60 bird species.
Birding mechanic: spot through binoculars, hold to 'study', species logged - the game hands you zoom binoculars before the first mission.
The species placement follows real South Florida ecology: waterbirds south, forest birds north, owls at night, real introduced exotics in the right spots.
The practical tip that emerges: find the habitat and the species follow - identical to real birding.

Documented inaccuracies: common Whooping Cranes (critically endangered in reality), Golden Eagles over nonexistent Florida mountains, renamed species to fit the fictional map (Black-capped for Carolina chickadee, 'New World Oriole').
Marketing said 62 birds; the official Progress screen lists 60 - the gap itself became community trivia.
The most accurate layer is the landscape: mangrove beaches, swamp grass, roadkill, fruit-stand typography - the stage convinces before the actors do.
items.why: You build worlds too - every reel, every frame. GTA 6's lesson transfers directly: believability is not detail-count, it is CONSISTENCY - put things where they ecologically, logically belong, and viewers feel a place instead of a backdrop. Break a rule only when your fiction's internal logic demands it.
items.example: Designing a market scene for a reel? Do what Rockstar's artists did: place elements by real-world logic - vegetable carts near the entrance, mechanic shops on the edge of town, pigeons on the electric wires at dusk - before adding anything flashy. The brain registers 'this place is real' from placement logic, not polygon count.

questions.q: What makes a game world's wildlife feel 'thought-out' rather than decorative?
questions.a: Ecological placement. GTA 6 puts waterbirds in southern coastal zones, forest birds north, owls out at night, and real introduced species where Florida birders actually find them - so the pattern holds up when a player tests it, which is exactly what Audubon's reviewer did.

questions.q: Why rename the chickadee instead of using the accurate species?
questions.a: Internal consistency wins over real-world accuracy: Carolina does not exist in the GTA universe, so a 'Carolina Chickadee' would break the fiction. The rule the designers follow is that the world must agree with itself, even when it disagrees with reality.

items.plain: The new GTA has 60 kinds of birds you can collect like Pokemon. A real birdwatcher found them all and discovered they live in the right neighborhoods - ducks by the coast, owls at night. Fake worlds feel real when everything is placed where it logically belongs.

items.headline: The second Riemann proof is 940 pages of human handwriting - and it is already bleeding
items.deck: Same day as the Alpöge-Claude release, a solo mathematician's 940-page manuscript claiming the GRANDER generalized Riemann Hypothesis went public - rushed out a year early. Within hours, reviewers found cracks. This is what open science at full speed actually looks like.
items.lead: On November 20, the same day as the Alpöge-Claude Lean release, Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted a 'hurried announcement': Alessandro Masullo's 940-page manuscript 'The Music of the Primes', claiming the generalized Riemann Hypothesis by purely human, classical means. John Carlos Baez's patient explainer, published November 22, walks through the strategy - and the problems found within hours.
items.body: The contrast is the story. Alpöge's proof exists as 17 million lines of machine-checked Lean, certified by the community on November 21. Masullo's is a human-scale manuscript in the tradition of Connes' trace-formula program: build a new formula for the logarithmic derivative of L-functions that visibly stays holomorphic - pole-free - up to the critical line, which forces every nontrivial zero onto it. It does not use Weil's positivity criterion, the route most attempts in this tradition take (the manuscript says so in boldface). The claim is even bigger than Alpöge's: the generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Hecke L-functions over general number fields. But the release was forced: Brian Conrad, who has read the manuscript for months, told Scientific American the plan was a full year of polishing before any announcement - Alpöge's claim made waiting impossible. Chapter 13, where GRH should finally be deduced, still contains placeholders. And the public stress test found issues within hours: an AI-assisted review organized by Eric Naslund argues a key theorem mispredicts a test case (expected log 2, but the stated limit conditions are unsatisfiable, giving 0); a separate checking effort flagged page 444, where a property of Schauder bases is extended to Markushevich bases, where it is false - and the false claim is used later. Baez's verdict is the balanced one: these objections may be fixable, the strategy is genuinely new and unlike Alpöge's (which transplants Stepanov's finite-field method with automorphic machinery), and even a failed attempt teaches where this dream breaks. Meanwhile a community Lean-formalization effort for Masullo's manuscript already has a progress map - 150 HN points of spectators watching the second race begin.
ptrs: Timeline: both proofs released November 20. Masullo's manuscript: 940 pages, human-written, claiming the GENERALIZED Riemann Hypothesis - a bigger claim than Alpöge's.
Posted by Ravi Vakil as a 'hurried announcement'; Brian Conrad says a full year of polishing was planned before Alpöge's claim forced early release.
Strategy: a new trace formula for L-functions, in Connes' program, explicitly NOT using Weil's positivity criterion (boldface in the manuscript).
Crack 1: an AI-assisted review organized by Eric Naslund says a key theorem predicts log 2 on a test case but its limit conditions are unsatisfiable - yielding 0.
Crack 2: page 444 extends a Schauder-basis property to Markushevich bases, where it is false; the false claim is used later in the manuscript.
Chapter 13 - where GRH should be deduced - still has placeholder text. Objections may be fixable; the paper is openly a draft.
Baez: the approach is genuinely novel and different from Alpöge's Stepanov-plus-automorphic route, so even fixing one proof would not make the other redundant.
A community Lean formalization of Masullo's manuscript already has a public progress map - HN discussion at 150 points (community reaction, not verification).
items.why: You just watched the two futures of mathematics collide in one weekend: a machine proof too big for any human to read, checked by other machines in 48 hours - and a human proof any expert can read, cracked in 48 hours by a swarm including AI reviewers. Whichever survives, the playbook for how big claims get tested has permanently changed - and you are studying for a career inside it.
items.example: Watch the two verification styles side by side: Alpöge's proof was certified by compiling and kernel-checking an export (binary verdict, fast). Masullo's is being reviewed by mathematicians reading arguments and AI reviewers probing test cases (incremental, judgment-heavy). When you ship your own work, you now know both gauntlets exist - formal checks for what machines can verify, adversarial human reading for what they cannot.

questions.q: Is the Riemann Hypothesis back to being unproven?
questions.a: No - these are two independent attempts. Alpöge's Lean proof was certified by the Lean and Mathlib communities on November 21 and stands. Masullo's separate manuscript claims the broader generalized RH but is an openly rough draft with reported flaws now under review.

questions.q: Why release a 940-page draft with placeholders?
questions.a: Priority pressure. Brian Conrad says the plan was a year of polishing, but Alpöge's November 20 claim made waiting impossible - in mathematics, being second to announce can cost priority for the result, so the draft went public unfinished.

questions.q: What is a trace formula, in one sentence?
questions.a: An identity that computes the same quantity two ways - once as a sum over 'spectral' data (here, zeros of the L-function) and once over 'geometric' data (here, primes) - so control of one side forces structure on the other.

items.plain: A second person claims to have solved the mega-puzzle from yesterday's story - his way uses 940 pages of pen-and-paper math instead of computer code. Because it came out a year early, sharp readers (and AI helpers) already found possible mistakes. Now everyone watches to see if the cracks can be patched.

items.headline: Put an AI in your house tonight - free, private, no terminal
items.deck: Unsloth Desktop is a free Windows app that serves open models through a chat interface - no Python, no commands, no subscription. Your 6GB card is below the comfy tier, but the offload trick means your 16GB of RAM quietly saves the day.
items.lead: A beginner's guide published November 22 walks through running your own local ChatGPT-style assistant on Windows using Unsloth Desktop - a free app, no terminal commands, about 10-15 minutes of setup. The catch for your exact hardware is real but workable, and the guide's own tables say why.
items.body: The setup is genuinely simple: install Unsloth Desktop (free), let it serve a model through a chat interface, pick a model sized to your GPU. The guide used an RTX 5090, but its tables are the useful part. Quantization shrinks models to lower precision - think of the same photo saved at 8, 4 and 2 bits: mostly the same picture, less detail. The guide's tiers: 8-12GB VRAM runs 9B-12B models; 16GB runs 14B and mixture-of-experts models up to 35B; 32GB runs 27B-35B at high quality. Your RTX 4050's 6GB sits below the first tier - so the honest recipe for YOUR machine tonight: pick a small model (a 3-4B-class Qwen at 4-bit, roughly 2.5GB) that fits the GPU entirely and runs fast, OR use the guide's key trick - mixture-of-experts models run only a few billion parameters per token, so the rest can live in system RAM. That is why the guide puts 35B MoE models in the 16GB row, quoting about 47 tokens/second for Qwen3.6-35B on a 16GB card. For Inkling 2 Mini specifically (yesterday's star): its quants run 10-11GB at 2-bit up to 24GB at 8-bit - the 2-bit file fits in your 16GB RAM with partial GPU offload, no 32GB upgrade required, just slower tokens. The privacy pitch: everything stays in the house, no usage limits, no subscription - and the whole family can use it on the home network.
ptrs: Unsloth Desktop: free Windows app, chat interface, no terminal or Python; setup 10-15 minutes plus model download time.
Quantization in one image: the same photo at 8, 4 and 2 bits - lower precision, smaller file, some quality loss; workloads differ in how much they care.
Guide's VRAM tiers: 8-12GB runs 9B-12B models; 16GB runs 14B + MoE up to 35B; 32GB runs 27B-35B comfortably with long context.
Your 6GB card is below tier one - your honest options: a 3-4B 4-bit model fully on GPU (fast), or MoE offload into your 16GB RAM (bigger brains, slower).
The MoE trick: only a few billion parameters fire per token, so the rest waits in system RAM - how a 35B model lands in the 16GB row at about 47 tokens/sec on the guide's test card.

Inkling 2 Mini on your machine: 2-bit build is 10-11GB total - fits your 16GB RAM with partial GPU offload today, no upgrade needed; the guide notes 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support, 1M-token context.

What you get: a private, free, no-limits assistant on your home network - the guide's framing is 'a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home', and the tradeoff versus the paid apps is speed and top-end quality.
items.why: This is the cheapest real upgrade to your AI workflow available: zero rupees, tonight, on hardware you already own. A local model handles the token-heavy grunt work - summarizing long PDFs, batch rewriting, private notes - without touching your usage limits on the paid apps you save for hard problems.
items.example: Tonight: install Unsloth Desktop, update it (Inkling needs a recent build), and pull a 4-bit 3-4B Qwen first - it fits your 6GB GPU whole and answers instantly, so you see the magic work. Then, if you want yesterday's reasoning model, download Inkling 2 Mini 2-bit and let it split between GPU and RAM - slower, but a frontier-adjacent brain living in your PC.

questions.q: Will a big model fry your 16GB RAM setup?
questions.a: No - the cost is speed, not safety. MoE models keep most weights in system RAM and fire only a few billion parameters per token; if the model plus context fits in RAM, it runs, just slower. The guide's own 35B-at-16GB row runs at about 47 tokens per second on a 16GB card.

questions.q: What do you actually lose versus paid ChatGPT or Claude?
questions.a: Top-end quality and speed. Local open models at consumer sizes trail the frontier apps on hard reasoning and polish; what you gain is privacy (nothing leaves the house), zero marginal cost, no usage caps, and always-on availability - which is why the guide frames it as offloading token-heavy routine work.

items.plain: You can run your own ChatGPT-like assistant on your PC for free with one app. Small models fit your graphics card directly; bigger ones can borrow your regular RAM to still work, just slower. Everything stays private in your house - like having a well instead of buying bottled water.

items.headline: A model that thinks in loops, and the honest map of where it runs
items.deck: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini is a 26.4B mixture-of-experts that only wakes 3.4B parameters per token and reuses its middle layers three times - and the community has already squeezed it to 5.4GB. Whether it runs on your PC depends on which door you take.
items.lead: Inkling 2 Mini, released November 20 by Thinking Machines Lab, is an open-weights reasoning model with an unusual trick: its middle layers loop three times per token instead of running once, so a small model gets extra thinking passes without extra weights. It leads every open-weights model under 100B parameters on two current benchmarks - and it has already been compressed small enough to matter for people without datacenter GPUs.
items.body: Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20 as open weights. The architecture is a looped mixture-of-experts transformer: 26.4 billion parameters total, but only 3.4 billion activate per token, and the middle block of layers runs three times per token, giving the model repeated passes over its own work. Counting the layers that actually fire, it touches about 5.4 billion weight-activations per token. On the DeepSWE v1.1 coding benchmark it scores 48.2% and on the Vals Index v2.2 it scores 46.5%, the best of any open-weights model under 100 billion parameters. The team also reports a variable-loop variant whose time horizon on agentic tasks without chain-of-thought grew from 16 seconds to 37 seconds at three loops, with no rise in agentic misbehavior. The honest hardware picture: the official NVFP4 weights are about 20GB, demonstrated on a 48GB MacBook Pro and NVIDIA's DGX Spark - not a 16GB Windows machine. A community member has published a 5.38GB build at 1.65 bits per weight that still scores 88.0% on GSM8K and 70.7% on HumanEval, beating larger community quants, but it is packed for Apple Silicon's MLX runtime only. For a Windows PC with 16GB RAM, the practical paths today are the 7.76GB Unsloth GGUF through llama.cpp on CPU (works, slowly) or running it hosted through Tinker, where Thinking Machines has made it available for inference and customization. The lab is also upfront about weak spots: multi-turn chat scores lag Qwen3.6-27B noticeably.
ptrs: Released November 20 by Thinking Machines Lab as open weights; also available on their Tinker platform for hosted inference and customization.
Architecture: looped transformer - the middle layers run three times per token. Mixture-of-experts: 26.4B total parameters, 3.4B active, about 5.4B weight-activations per token.
Leads all open-weights models under 100B on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and the Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%).

A variable-loop variant grew its no-chain-of-thought time horizon on agentic tasks from 16 seconds to 37 seconds at 3 loops, with shorter but still legible reasoning traces and no measured rise in agentic sabotage.
Official NVFP4 weights are about 20GB - the lab demoed them building a flight sim and a 20-agent village offline on a 48GB MacBook Pro. Not a fit for 16GB RAM plus 6GB VRAM today.
A community 'LookAtMyQuant' build squeezes the 18.89GB weights to 5.38GB (1.65 bits per weight) and still hits GSM8K 88.0% and HumanEval 70.7% - but it runs only on Apple Silicon via MLX.
On a Windows PC the workable routes are the 7.76GB Unsloth GGUF on CPU through llama.cpp inside 16GB RAM (slow but real), or hosted on Tinker at full quality.
Known weak spots, from the lab itself: multi-turn chat (50.0% on MultiChallenge) and complex instruction following (33.4%), both behind Qwen3.6-27B.
items.why: Local models keep shrinking toward your hardware, and this is the clearest sign yet: a frontier-lab reasoning model whose community quant would idle in a corner of your RAM. The catch is just as useful to know - the tiny build is Mac-only, so your honest path today is a CPU GGUF or the hosted version, and the 32GB upgrade question stays exactly that: a question.
items.example: Say you want to test it tonight without spending anything: download the 7.76GB Unsloth GGUF, run it with llama.cpp on CPU with the context at 8K, and ask it to debug a small Python script. Expect seconds per token, not chat-app speed - but you are running a current open-weights reasoning leader on a 16GB machine.

questions.q: How does a 3.4B-active model beat much bigger ones?
questions.a: Two multipliers stack: mixture-of-experts keeps only 3.4B parameters firing per token while 26.4B exist to specialize, and the looped middle layers give each token three passes through the model's core reasoning block. Thinking Machines' own variable-loop experiments show more loops buying longer task horizons without extra weights.

questions.q: Can you run the 5.38GB version on your RTX 4050 PC?
questions.a: No - that build is packed for Apple's MLX runtime and only runs on Apple Silicon. Your Windows path is the 7.76GB GGUF on CPU via llama.cpp (fits 16GB RAM, runs slowly) or Tinker's hosted version. The official ~20GB weights would be 32GB-upgrade territory and even then target Mac and DGX-class runtimes.

questions.q: Where does it still lose?
questions.a: Multi-turn conversation and complex constraints. The lab's own numbers put it at 50.0% on MultiChallenge and 33.4% on ComplexConstraints, behind Qwen3.6-27B. It is a reasoning engine first, a chatbot second.

items.plain: A new open model gets big-brain results from small parts by reusing its middle layers three times per token. The famous 5.4GB shrunk version only works on Macs. On your Windows PC, use the 7.76GB version on CPU (slow) or the hosted one. Great at reasoning, mediocre at long chats.

items.headline: One number that sizes every headline you will ever set
items.deck: Pick a base size, pick a ratio, multiply - that is a modular scale, the quiet math behind type systems that feel inevitable instead of arbitrary. Designers have leaned on it since the Renaissance; your CSS can lean on it tonight.
items.lead: A modular type scale is a row of font sizes where each step is the previous one times a fixed ratio - base times ratio to the power of n. Instead of guessing that a headline feels about right at 42px, you pick a ratio like 1.25 and let the ladder generate every size in the system, so headings, body and captions all share one hidden rhythm.
items.body: The idea, laid out in a recent essay by designer Rasmus Starck, is almost suspiciously simple: choose a base size (say 16px) and a ratio (say 1.25), and every size in your design is base x ratio^n - 16, 20, 25, 31, 39, and so on. The practice is old: Robert Bringhurst's The Elements of Typographic Style documents classical scales from 6 to 72 points that printers used for centuries, built on ratios that echo musical harmony. Tim Brown's 2011 A List Apart essay 'More Meaningful Typography' revived the idea for the web and shipped modularscale.com to compute the ladders. The practical payoff is consistency: every size on the page is related to every other by the same multiplier, so the design feels tuned rather than assembled. The modern wrinkle is context - a ratio that sings on a big monitor crowds a phone, so many designers run a gentler ratio for small screens and a bolder one for large ones. In CSS this is now a few custom properties and calc() away, no framework required.
ptrs: The formula: size(n) = base x ratio^n. Base 16px with ratio 1.25 gives 16, 20, 25, 31.25, 39 - a ladder, not a guess.
The lineage is real: Bringhurst documents classical type scales (6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 16, 18, 21, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72pt) rooted in centuries of printing and musical proportion.
Tim Brown's 2011 A List Apart article 'More Meaningful Typography' brought the idea to the web; his modularscale.com calculator still generates scales from a base and ratio.
Ratio is the taste knob: small ratios (1.125-1.2) give subtle, text-heavy hierarchy; big ratios (1.414 and up) give dramatic poster contrast.
Screen size changes the answer: a wide ratio crowds a phone, so a common pattern is ~1.2 for mobile and ~1.333+ for desktop, switched in one media query.
In modern CSS the whole system is three custom properties and calc(): --base, --ratio, and sizes computed as var() chains - no preprocessor needed.
items.why: You tweak designs constantly, and this kills a whole category of fiddling: once a scale exists, 'how big should this heading be' stops being a vibe decision and becomes a rung on a ladder. It is also the difference between a page that looks designed and one that looks decorated.
items.example: Tonight: open any page you have styled, set --base: 1rem and --ratio: 1.25, then define --s1: calc(var(--base) * var(--ratio)), --s2: calc(var(--s1) * var(--ratio)) and so on, and swap your hardcoded heading sizes for the variables. If the hierarchy feels timid on desktop, bump the ratio to 1.333 inside one media query and watch the whole page retune itself.

questions.q: Why multiply instead of adding a fixed number of pixels?
questions.a: Because perception is proportional: the jump from 12px to 16px reads as big, while 40px to 44px barely registers. Multiplying by a ratio keeps each step feeling like the same-size move at every level of the scale - the same reason musical intervals are ratios, not fixed frequency gaps.

questions.q: Which ratio should you start with?
questions.a: 1.25 (the 'major third') is the standard safe start: enough hierarchy to feel deliberate, gentle enough for text-heavy pages. Go 1.125 for dense dashboards, 1.333 or 1.414 when you want poster-like contrast - and consider a smaller ratio on phones, where big steps run out of width fast.

items.plain: Choose a base font size and a multiplier; every size on the page is the base times the multiplier again and again. It is a centuries-old printing trick, it makes pages feel tuned, and it is three lines of CSS.

items.headline: Why some movie sound belongs to the world, and some to you
items.deck: Dialogue, footsteps, a radio playing in the kitchen - sound the characters can hear is diegetic. The score swelling over the mountains is not. The border between them is one of cinema's oldest tricks, and editors cross it on purpose.
items.lead: Diegetic sound is any sound that exists inside the story's world - dialogue, footsteps, doors, a song on a car radio - while non-diegetic sound exists only for the audience: the orchestral score, narration, stylized whooshes. A new primer from sound-design toolmaker Krotos walks through how the two layers are built, and how films blur the line on purpose.
items.body: The vocabulary is simple, the craft is not. Diegetic sound comes from inside the storyworld: what characters say and what their world does - dialogue, Foley footsteps, offscreen traffic that implies a city without showing it. Non-diegetic sound is commentary aimed at you alone: the score, a narrator's voice, the sub-bass boom under a title card. Sound teams make diegetic audio believable by giving it the room it claims to live in - reverb that matches the hall, the muffled smallness of a phone speaker, panning that tracks a car across the frame. Blade Runner 2049 is a favorite example of heavy Foley craft, with every footstep and fabric move performed to picture. The sophisticated move is the trans-diegetic transition: a needle drops on a record inside the scene, and a beat later the same song becomes the full score, sliding from the characters' world into yours without a cut. Editors use it to hand emotion between the story and the audience so smoothly you never notice the border crossing.
ptrs: Diegetic = inside the storyworld: dialogue, Foley (performed footsteps, cloth, props), and ambience from sources the scene implies, even offscreen.
Non-diegetic = audience-only: the musical score, narration, and stylized sound effects that no character can hear.
Believability comes from space cues: reverb matched to the room, speaker emulation for phones and radios, panning that follows onscreen motion.
Blade Runner 2049 is a reference case for dense Foley - nearly everything you hear was performed and recorded to picture.
Offscreen diegetic sound is a budget-free storytelling device: a siren or a dog bark builds a world bigger than the frame.
Trans-diegetic transitions blur the border on purpose: a song starts on a character's radio and swells into the score, carrying a scene's emotion into the audience's layer.
The Krotos primer (February 2026) frames the split as the first decision in any sound build: what does the world say, and what do we say about it?
items.why: You shoot and cut video; this is the cheapest production-value upgrade that exists. Record three seconds of room tone, add the right reverb to a phone voice, let one song escape the scene and become your score - viewers can't name what improved, but the edit feels expensive.
items.example: In your next reel: find the moment your background track starts, and instead of fading it in, let it begin as a tinny speaker inside the shot for two seconds - a phone, a shop radio - then bloom it to full quality as the cut lands. You have just done the trans-diegetic trick that trailers charge money for.

questions.q: Is a character's voiceover diegetic or not?
questions.a: Usually non-diegetic - narration is aimed at the audience and the other characters can't hear it. The exception is when the voice is anchored in the world: a phone call, a letter read aloud, an announcer in a stadium. The test is always 'can anyone inside the story hear this?'

questions.q: Why do phone voices in films sound thin?
questions.a: That thin, band-limited sound is deliberate speaker emulation - the mixer filters the voice to match what a real phone speaker would produce. It is one of the space cues that makes a diegetic sound feel anchored in the world instead of pasted on top of it.

items.plain: Sound the characters can hear is diegetic; sound only you hear is the score. Good films fake rooms with reverb and panning, and the slickest move is a song that starts inside the scene and quietly becomes the soundtrack.

items.info_caption: The border is the decision. Sounds live inside the world or outside it - and directors smuggle them across when it serves the story.

items.headline: The Riemann proof now carries the Lean community's stamp
items.deck: Yesterday we told you about the claim. Today the people who guard the proof assistant itself spoke: the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative say they have full confidence Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct - 17 million lines of machine-checked mathematics.
items.lead: The Lean and Mathlib communities have issued a joint statement - endorsed by both the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative - saying they have full confidence that Leander Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. It is the strongest possible response to yesterday's claim, and it came with a public list of exactly what was checked.
items.body: Yesterday's story was a claim; today's is a certification. In a November 21 blog post, the Lean and Mathlib communities - speaking jointly through the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, the two bodies that maintain the proof assistant and its mathematical library - state: 'We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct.' The verification runs to about 17 million lines of Lean, and the post details the four criteria that were checked: the formal statement is Mathlib's own vetted definition of the Riemann Hypothesis, not a lookalike; the entire library compiles, and dozens of people have independently reproduced the build; the proved theorem was matched against the official statement with a dedicated comparator tool; and the raw proof export was re-checked by multiple independent verification kernels, including con-leche and con-ron, which carry their own formal proofs that they cannot accept a false proof. An accessible overview of the mathematics is hosted by Drew Sutherland at MIT. The Hacker News discussion ran to 836 points and 688 comments, and the community's own caveat is worth quoting: formal certainty is not the same as human understanding, and the work of digesting the ideas is only starting.
ptrs: Joint statement published November 21, endorsed by both the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative - the maintainers of the proof assistant and its library, respectively.

Who proved it: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, built the proof working with Anthropic's Claude - Nature, Scientific American and The Guardian all center the human-plus-AI collaboration. Sutherland's MIT checks were also run with Claude Code.
The sentence that matters: 'We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct.'
Scale: about 17 million lines of Lean code compiled as part of the verification.
Check 1 - the statement: the proved proposition is Mathlib's vetted RiemannHypothesis definition, so it is the real conjecture, not a weakened paraphrase.
Check 2 - the build: the library compiles from scratch, and dozens of people reproduced the compile independently.
Check 3 - the match: a comparator tool plus con-leche --compare verified the proved theorem is exactly the Mathlib statement.
Check 4 - independent kernels: the raw proof export was re-verified by multiple independent checkers, including con-leche and con-ron, which carry formal proofs of their own soundness.
The community's own caveat: machine-checked correctness is settled; human understanding of the ideas is the next project. Drew Sutherland (MIT) hosts an accessible overview of the mathematics.

Independent public tracker: Andrew 'Drew' Sutherland (MIT) is re-running the verification in the open - as of early November 22 (UTC), two independently written kernels (nanoda, con-leche) accept the full exported proof and a sandboxed rebuild reproduces the 61.5GB export byte for byte; final confirmation replays were still running.
items.why: This is the pattern to remember for every future 'AI helps solve famous problem' headline: the claim, then the independent machine audit, then the human verdict. The Riemann Hypothesis - 167 years open, a million-dollar Clay prize - just cleared all three gates in public, with receipts you can re-run yourself.
items.example: You can inspect the certificate chain yourself: the community blog post links the comparator output and the independent-kernel checkers (con-leche, con-ron), and the Mathlib statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is a few lines of readable Lean. Even without following the math, reading what was checked is a masterclass in how to verify a claim properly.

questions.q: Who exactly is vouching here?
questions.a: Not the prover and not a journalist: the Lean FRO (the organization that builds the Lean proof assistant) and the Mathlib Initiative (the community that maintains its mathematics library). They are the people with the most to lose from endorsing a wrong proof, and they published their checking criteria with the endorsement.

questions.q: How can software certify 17 million lines?
questions.a: By checking exports, not trust: the proof produces a raw certificate file, and small independent programs - some, like con-leche and con-ron, with their own machine-checked proofs that they cannot accept a false theorem - re-verify every step. Compilers and comparators confirm the theorem being proved is literally Mathlib's Riemann Hypothesis.

questions.q: Is the million-dollar prize paid out now?
questions.a: Not automatically. The Clay Institute has its own rules and human review process for the Millennium Prize. The Lean certification settles machine-checkable correctness; the prize committee's judgment, and the community's deeper reading of the ideas, are separate and still ahead.

items.plain: The people who maintain the Lean proof system checked yesterday's claimed Riemann Hypothesis proof four different ways - right statement, clean compile, exact match, independent re-verification - and now say they are fully confident it is correct. The machines are convinced; humans are still reading.

items.info_alt: Horizontal pipeline diagram: paper stack, arrow, cobalt gear, arrow, two magnifying glasses, arrow, vermilion seal with checkmark
items.info_caption: Four gates, all public: the statement is Mathlib's own, the library compiles, a comparator matches theorem to statement, and independent kernels re-check every step.

items.headline: Prove 2 + 2 = 4 like a mathematician, in your browser
items.deck: Lean - the same proof assistant that just certified the Riemann Hypothesis - runs free in a browser tab. No install, no signup: type one line, watch a computer accept your proof, then break it and watch it refuse.
items.lead: The Lean community maintains an online playground where the full proof assistant runs in your browser. It is the exact tool behind today's 17-million-line Riemann verification, scaled down to a text box - and a three-line exercise gives you the real sensation of a machine checking your logic.
items.body: Proof assistants are usually an afternoon of installers and toolchain wrangling. Lean's community cuts that to zero: their homepage links a live online version of Lean that runs in the browser, no account needed. The sensation to chase is the compiler's verdict. Type 'example : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl' and run it - rfl is Lean's 'this is true by computation' proof, and the checker accepts silently. Now change the 4 to a 5 and run again: the same tool that just certified the Riemann Hypothesis rejects your claim, with an error pointing at the lie. That refusal is the entire idea of formal verification in miniature. For a second hit, prove something genuinely non-obvious - that addition commutes for all natural numbers: 'example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := Nat.add_comm a b'. You have just reused a theorem from Mathlib, the same library the Riemann proof builds on. And if you want the machine to do the work, try 'example : 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 := by omega' - the omega tactic solves arithmetic goals by itself.
ptrs: The Lean community homepage links a browser version of Lean - no install, no signup, the same proof assistant used for the Riemann verification.
Exercise 1: type 'example : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl' and run it. rfl proves things that are true by direct computation.
Exercise 2: change the 4 to a 5. The checker refuses with an error - the same mechanism that would catch a false step in a million-line proof.
Exercise 3: prove a real theorem for ALL natural numbers: 'example (a b : Nat) : a + b = b + a := Nat.add_comm a b'. You just cited Mathlib, the library under today's Riemann certification.
Exercise 4: let the machine prove arithmetic itself with 'example : 2 + 3 * 4 = 14 := by omega'.
Ten minutes, zero setup, and you have touched the exact verification stack from today's lead story.
items.why: You have read about formal verification twice in two days; this converts the headline into a hand-feel in ten minutes. Once a proof checker has rejected your deliberate lie, you understand the Riemann certification better than most people commenting on it.
items.example: Do it now: open the Lean community homepage, click through to the online version, paste 'example : 2 + 2 = 4 := rfl', run it, then corrupt the 4 into a 5 and run again. The error message is the whole point - software that cannot be flattered into accepting a wrong claim.

questions.q: What is rfl actually doing?
questions.a: rfl stands for reflexivity - it proves goals of the form 'X = X' by having Lean compute both sides down to the same thing. When you write 2 + 2 = 4, Lean evaluates 2 + 2, gets 4, sees 4 = 4, and accepts. When you write 2 + 2 = 5, the computation produces 4, 4 is not 5, and there is no proof to give.

questions.q: Is the browser version the real thing?
questions.a: Yes - it runs the genuine Lean toolchain compiled for the web, not a toy simulator. The same kernel design that checks your one-liner is what independent verifiers just used on the 17-million-line Riemann proof; only the scale differs.

items.plain: The proof software from today's big story runs free in a browser tab. Type a one-line proof, watch it accepted, then write a false statement and watch the machine refuse. That refusal is why the Riemann certification means something.

items.headline: Hum a Tune, This Tiny Model Writes Down the Notes
items.deck: Dettato turns any recording into a MIDI file with a model so small it sounds like a typo - 20 million parameters beating models 65 times its size. And yes, it clears your 6GB GPU without breaking a sweat.
items.lead: Dettato is a new open-source audio-to-MIDI transcription model from kobimusic: feed it a song or a recording of you humming, and it spits out the notes as a MIDI file you can drop into any music app. The wild part is the size - at 20M parameters it is roughly 65x smaller than MuScriptor 1.3B, the previous best open model, and it still beats it on every published benchmark.
items.body: Dettato is a new open-source audio-to-MIDI transcription model from kobimusic: feed it a song or a recording of you humming, and it spits out the notes as a MIDI file you can drop into any music app. The wild part is the size. At 20M parameters it is roughly 65x smaller than MuScriptor 1.3B, the previous best open model, and it still beats it on every published benchmark: composite score 60.8 against MuScriptor's 47.4, and even a nose ahead of mirelo's closed-source A2M v1.1 Pro at 56.1. The training story is just as sharp: the model was trained on absolutely no copyrighted recordings, using synthetic instrument audio and Creative Commons solo instruments from the URMP dataset blended with about 20 soundfonts, and the outputs are cleared for commercial use. Setup is two lines: pip install git+https://github.com/kobimusic/dettato, then run dettato song.mp3 -o out/ and you get out/song.mid plus a JSON of the notes; the weights download from Hugging Face on first run, and it needs Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.2+. A CUDA GPU is recommended but not demanding: on an RTX 5060 8GB a 4-minute song transcribes in about 15 seconds while peaking under 4GB of GPU memory, which means your RTX 4050 with 6GB fits comfortably; the CPU path works but is slow, with a 15-second clip taking 87 seconds on a laptop CPU. Keep the honest limits in view: dettato gives you performance MIDI - the right notes at the right times - not engraved sheet music, and the author himself points you to Songscription or Klangio if you need printable scores; splitting overlapping instruments correctly is a known weak spot, and m4a or aac files need ffmpeg installed. Bro, this is the suit-up moment for anyone making short-form video: original background music from your own humming, no licensing anxiety, running locally for free.
ptrs: Open-source audio-to-MIDI model from kobimusic, released November 16 - recording in, MIDI file out, and commercial use of the output is explicitly allowed.
20M parameters, about 65x smaller than MuScriptor 1.3B, yet ahead on every published metric: composite 60.8 vs 47.4, and just past mirelo's closed A2M v1.1 Pro at 56.1.
Trained on zero copyrighted recordings - synthetic instruments plus CC solo recordings from URMP and around 20 soundfonts.

Two-line setup: pip install git+https://github.com/kobimusic/dettato, then dettato song.mp3 -o out/ gives out/song.mid and out/song.json; weights auto-download from Hugging Face; needs Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.2+.
Fits your rig: on an RTX 5060 8GB a 4-minute song takes ~15 seconds under 4GB VRAM, so a 6GB RTX 4050 is fine; CPU works but crawls (15s of audio took 87s on a laptop CPU).

Known limits: it writes performance MIDI (notes and timing), not sheet music - the author recommends Songscription or Klangio for that; instrument separation can wobble; m4a/aac inputs need ffmpeg on the PATH.
items.why: You make reels, and background music is the eternal headache - stock tracks are overused, licensed tracks cost money. Record yourself humming a hook, run it through this, assign any instrument in a free DAW, and the track is yours, legally clean because the model never touched a copyrighted recording. It runs on your PC today, no upgrade needed.
items.example: Hum a 20-second melody into your phone for a TechBlast reel intro. Copy the file to your PC, run dettato hook.mp3 -o out/, open out/hook.mid in a free DAW like Cakewalk, swap the piano-roll onto a synth patch, and export - an original intro sting, cleared for monetized videos.

questions.q: How can a 20M model beat a 1.3B one?
questions.a: The author treats transcription as a local pitch-lane problem with a purpose-built architecture instead of throwing a giant general model at it - and says the copyright-free training constraint pushed them toward better design rather than holding them back.

questions.q: Will it run on your 16GB / RTX 4050 6GB machine?
questions.a: Yes. The README shows a 4-minute song peaking under 4GB of GPU memory on an RTX 5060 8GB, so 6GB VRAM is comfortable; CPU-only works too, just much slower.

questions.q: Can you use the MIDI it makes in a monetized video?
questions.a: Yes - the model is open source and its outputs are explicitly cleared for commercial purposes, and no copyrighted recordings were used in training.

items.plain: When you hum a song, a computer normally has no idea which notes you sang. This tool listens and writes down the notes, like a friend with perfect hearing jotting sheet music while you sing - except the friend is a tiny program that fits in a corner of your graphics card. Because it is small and free, anyone can use it, not just big studios.

items.headline: If Everything Shouts, Nobody Hears Anything
items.deck: A developer measured a page where 19 of 20 texts were bold - and the price was the single weakest element. The fix was not louder design. It was quieter everything.
items.lead: Visual hierarchy means arranging a screen so the eye reads it in the same order the user needs it - and the counterintuitive first move is to calm almost everything down, not to pump one thing up. A teardown of an online bookstore's page shows the failure perfectly: nearly every line was bold and colorful, and the price, the one thing every buyer hunts for, was the weakest text on the page.
items.body: Visual hierarchy means arranging a screen so the eye reads it in the same order the user needs it - and the counterintuitive first move is to calm almost everything down, not to pump one thing up. Mert Özen's teardown of an online bookstore's book page shows the failure perfectly. The before page grew request by request: marketing wanted the shipping banner visible, someone wanted the author linked, someone else wanted ratings purple, until 19 of the 20 text elements were bold and all four buttons were identical solid blue. Measured with a script, the price sat at 16 pixels and regular weight - literally the least-emphasized text on the page - while the ISBN was the same size and heavier. The fix rebuilt the page in three levels: level one is what the page is (the book title, bumped from 22 to 32 pixels), level two is where the user decides and acts (price, stock, Add to cart, with the price at 28 pixels bold), level three is lookup-only metadata (ISBN, publisher, page count) in small regular grey. After the rebuild only 6 of 21 text elements were bold. Four tools do the work: size (few and clear steps - 16 vs 17 pixels reads as inconsistency, not hierarchy), weight (cheaper than size, so use it sparingly), colour (give every colour a job - dark grey for main text at 17.73:1 contrast, mid grey for secondary at 7.55:1, blue for clickable, green for stock) and position (top and left get seen first). The Gestalt principles explain grouping: proximity, similarity, common region, continuity and figure/ground tell the eye what belongs together - on the broken page, the stock line was spaced exactly like the metadata and vanished into it. And the famous F-shaped scanning pattern is a symptom, not a goal: when a page gives no hierarchy, users fall back on lazy scanning and miss the right side; a page with clear levels gets read heading to heading, the layer-cake pattern. Challenge accepted: open anything you designed recently, squint at it, and if you can not instantly name the one most important element, you know what to do.
ptrs: Hierarchy = the eye's reading order matching the user's task order; three levels are enough: what the page is, where the user decides and acts, supporting lookup info.
The failure mode is accumulated emphasis: the bookstore page hit 19 of 20 texts bold and four identical solid buttons, so the price was the weakest element and the eye went to an orange banner first.
The first fix is calming, not enlarging: turning metadata from bold black to regular grey moved the needle more than making the price bigger; after the fix only 6 of 21 elements stayed bold.

Four tools, in order of bluntness: size (few, clear steps), weight (use sparingly), colour (assign roles - main text 17.73:1 contrast, secondary 7.55:1, one colour for clickable, one for status), position (top and left first).
Gestalt principles decide grouping: proximity, similarity, common region, continuity and figure/ground - identical spacing made the stock info vanish into the metadata list on the broken page.
NN/g's F-pattern is a symptom of weak hierarchy, not a design goal; clear levels flip scanning into the layer-cake pattern where users jump heading to heading.
items.why: Every poster, thumbnail and landing page you touch wins or loses in the first second. This is the cheapest skill multiplier there is: no new software, no new fonts, just demote everything that is not the point - and suddenly the thing that matters finally reads.
items.example: Take a reel cover you made. Turn every text except the title to regular weight and mid grey, make the title twice as big, and move the one action (follow, watch, buy) into its own tinted box. Squint: if the title and the action are the only things that survive the blur, you nailed it.

questions.q: Why did making the price bigger not fix the page?
questions.a: Emphasis only works against a calm background - with 19 of 20 texts bold, one more bold line goes unnoticed, so the fix started by quieting everything else down.

questions.q: What are the three hierarchy levels?
questions.a: Level one says what the page is, level two is where the user decides and acts, level three is supporting information people look up only when they need it.

questions.q: Is the F-pattern something to design for?
questions.a: No - NN/g calls it a symptom, not a goal: users fall back on it when the page gives no hierarchy; strong hierarchy produces heading-to-heading layer-cake scanning instead.

items.plain: Imagine a room where everyone shouts at once - you cannot pick out a single voice. A page where everything is big and bold is that room. Design works when one thing speaks loudly, a few things speak normally, and everything else whispers, so visitors instantly know where to look first.
