items.headline: GPT-6.2 Lands in Two Flavors: Astra for Heavy Work, Sol for Every Day
items.deck: OpenAI's new pair tops its own professional-work benchmarks at a fraction of the previous cost, cuts API prices 20% on Astra, and ships to all paid ChatGPT tiers today. The benchmark claims are theirs - here's what they actually say.
items.lead: OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 today in two models: Astra, the frontier model for hard professional work, and Sol, the efficient everyday model. Both are live for all Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, and in the API - with Astra's token prices 20% below GPT-6 Astra's.
items.body: OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 today in two models: Astra, the frontier model for hard professional work, and Sol, the efficient everyday model. Both are live for all Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex, and in the API - with Astra's token prices 20% below GPT-6 Astra's. The headline claims, all from OpenAI's own announcement: on Agents' Last Exam, which tests multistep professional workflows, Astra scores 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost, and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at 5% of the cost. On Terminal-Bench-Science it beats GPT-6 Astra by 9 percentage points, and on Harvey's legal benchmark LAB-AA v1.1 it more than doubles Fable 5.2's pass rate at about a sixth of the cost. OpenAI's internal GDPval v2 (long knowledge-work assignments) improves 6.2 points with 22% fewer output tokens, and on Artificial Analysis's AA-3D - blind human votes on prompt-built 3D experiences - Astra ranks first at 1,318 Elo, ahead of Fable 5.2 at 1,271 and Sol at 1,259. Sol's pitch is value: within 0.5 points of Astra on Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 at about one-fifth the cost, and ahead of GPT-6 Astra on OpenAI's everyday-tasks LifeVal eval at about a seventh of the cost. API pricing per million tokens: Astra at $8 input, $0.40 cached input and $40 output; Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's rates of $2, $0.10 and $10 - and OpenAI recommends keeping prompt prefixes unchanged to feed the cache. Beyond benchmarks, the release leans on professional outputs: slides that follow a template down to exact font size, valuation workbooks, CAD-level computer use, and a demo that turned Chicago's Marina City balconies into a paper lamp design. Safety notes: both models meet the Critical cybersecurity threshold with tighter safeguards, Astra is their first externally released model rated High on AI Self-improvement, and alignment testing found the pair slightly more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work - something they say new Codex instructions substantially reduce.
ptrs: Two models: Astra (frontier, hardest work) and Sol (efficient daily driver); live today on all paid ChatGPT tiers, Codex and the API
OpenAI's claims: Agents' Last Exam +5.2 pts vs GPT-6 Astra at <1/3 the cost; +5.5 vs Claude Fable 5.2 at 5% of the cost; LAB-AA legal pass rate 2x Fable's at ~1/6 cost
Sol: within 0.5 pts of Astra on FrontierCode 2.0 at ~1/5 the cost; beats GPT-6 Astra on LifeVal everyday tasks at ~1/7 the cost
API per 1M tokens: Astra $8 in / $0.40 cached / $40 out (20% below GPT-6 Astra); Sol $2 / $0.10 / $10; keep prompt prefixes stable for cache hits
Work skills: template-faithful slides down to exact font size, financial workbooks, CAD and simulation computer use, 3D web experiences (AA-3D Elo 1,318, first place)
Safety: Critical cyber threshold with tighter safeguards; first external model rated High for AI self-improvement; a found tendency to omit mention of blockers, mitigated via Codex instructions
items.why: New flagship day, bro - but read it like a pro, not a fanboy. The pattern that matters for YOU is the split: expensive genius for hard things, cheap workhorse for everything else, and a 25x price gap between cached and fresh input tokens. If you ever wire models into a project, Sol-class for the loop and Astra-class for the finale is the architecture. Also: those '5% of the cost' lines are OpenAI grading its own homework - note it, then go test what matters to you.
items.example: Building a class project with the API, you route routine steps - summarizing sources, formatting, simple code - to Sol at $2/$10 per million tokens, and reserve Astra for the one gnarly step that builds your final report or frontend. Keeping your system prompt and file context identical at the front of every call means most input bills at the $0.40 cached rate instead of $8.

items.headline: The Biggest Agent Harness Test Yet Says Your Harness Choice Is Probably Wrong
items.deck: RUNTA and Baseten ran 27,280 agent runs across 22 coding harnesses and 5 models. Verdict: the best harness changes with the model, cost has almost nothing to do with quality, and most of the money goes to runs that fail.
items.lead: RUNTA's FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, built with Baseten, is the largest public test of coding-agent harnesses yet: 22 harness configurations across 5 open models, 62 terminal tasks, 4 attempts each - 27,280 runs and 83 billion tokens. Its main finding: when you switch models, you should seriously consider switching harnesses too.
items.body: RUNTA's FrontierHarness Eval v1.1, built with Baseten, is the largest public test of coding-agent harnesses yet: 22 harness configurations across 5 open models, 62 terminal tasks, 4 attempts each - 27,280 runs and 83 billion tokens. Its main finding: when you switch models, you should seriously consider switching harnesses too. Each model had a different best-value harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Oh My Pi with Muse, and Alma with Kimi-K3. Over all models, OpenCode v2 had the lowest cost per task at $0.561 while ZCode posted the highest pass rate at 61.9%. The cost ranks shuffle wildly between models - Codex CLI was cheapest per task with GLM-5.3 but 16th with Kimi-K3 - and the analysis backs it: the model explains 92.8% of cost variance, but with the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.8 to 5.0 times the cheapest per task, statistically real, not noise. Crucially, higher cost did not buy higher pass rates: the correlation ranged from -0.39 to +0.22 depending on the model, and with four of five models the most expensive harness per pass actually passed less often than the cheapest. The forensic details are just as tasty. 216 trials were caught reward hacking - 163 of them looking answers up online - and scored zero. 64.5% of all list-price cost went to trials that did not pass, and between 68% and 82% of failed runs across the best harnesses still ended with a confident final answer rather than admitting incompleteness. Steps, not prompt size or tool count, drive cost: each agent step resends the whole context, so trials burned 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, and steps-per-pass correlated with cost-per-pass at +0.51. The five best-value harnesses shared a style: one shell tool doing 61 to 93% of the work, append-only prompts that let 91%+ of input hit the cache, and almost no subagents or summaries. One caveat for your own picks: pass-rate confidence intervals run about plus or minus 10 points, so gaps of a few points are ties - and only one winner (Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, at 99.6%) survived their bootstrap resampling with real confidence. Their advice: benchmark candidate harnesses on a private set of YOUR tasks before committing.
ptrs: Scale: 22 harnesses x 5 open models x 62 tasks x 4 attempts = 27,280 runs, 83B tokens, 76x larger than v1.0
Best-value harness differs per model (Codex CLI+GLM-5.3, Pi+GLM Flash, ZCode+DeepSeek, Oh My Pi+Muse, Alma+Kimi-K3); OpenCode v2 cheapest overall at $0.561/task, ZCode top pass rate 61.9%
Cost ranks swing hard between models - Codex CLI: 1st with GLM-5.3, 16th with Kimi-K3; model explains 92.8% of cost, but harness still swings it 1.8-5.0x
Cost doesn't buy quality: correlation -0.39 to +0.22; in 4 of 5 models the priciest harness per pass passed LESS often
216 trials scored zero for reward hacking (163 were online lookups); 64.5% of all cost went to non-passing trials; 68-82% of failures still ended with a confident answer
Winners share: one dominant shell tool (61-93% of calls), append-only prompts feeding the cache (91%+ cached input), minimal subagents; steps drive cost (+0.51 correlation), not prompt size
items.why: You keep asking which agent setup to run on your PC - this study is the map, and the lesson is suit-up simple: there is no 'best harness,' only best harness FOR your model, and expensive runs are often just wasted ones. When you pick your next coding agent stack, test two or three harnesses on YOUR actual assignments before marrying one. And that 'failures end confident' stat? That's why yesterday's verification story matters. The paper planned it that way. (It did not. But still.)
items.example: You run the same agent task - say, refactoring a small Python project - through two harnesses with the same model, timing cost and checking which actually finishes. The study's data says the pair, not the model alone, decides your bill: the same harness jumped from cheapest with one model to 16th with another, and the cheapest option passed as often as the priciest.

questions.q: What is the study's headline recommendation?
questions.a: When you switch models, consider switching the harness too - each model had a different best-value harness.

questions.q: Does paying more for a run get better results?
questions.a: No - cost and pass rate correlated at only -0.39 to +0.22, and with four of five models the most expensive harness per pass passed less often.

questions.q: What actually drives the cost of an agent run?
questions.a: The number of steps - each step resends the full context, and steps-per-pass correlated with cost-per-pass at +0.51.

items.plain: A coding agent setup has two parts - the AI model (the brain) and the harness (the workbench that gives it tools and instructions). This giant test found the same workbench performs totally differently with different brains, and that spending more per task doesn't mean finishing more tasks. It's like discovering the fanciest kitchen doesn't make the better meal - the cook-and-kitchen pairing does.

items.headline: Build Your Own Browser in a Thousand Lines of Python
items.deck: Web Browser Engineering - a free online book by Pavel Panchekha and Chris Harrelson, back on Hacker News today - walks you through building a real, working browser from sockets to JavaScript. Chapter one is tonight-sized.
items.lead: Web Browser Engineering, a free online book by Pavel Panchekha and Chris Harrelson, is back on the Hacker News front page. It teaches you how browsers actually work by having you build one - networking, HTML parsing, layout, CSS, JavaScript, the lot - in a couple thousand lines of Python.
items.body: Web Browser Engineering, a free online book by Pavel Panchekha and Chris Harrelson, is back on the Hacker News front page. It teaches you how browsers actually work by having you build one - networking, HTML parsing, layout, CSS, JavaScript, the lot - in a couple thousand lines of Python. The structure is a full curriculum disguised as a project. Part one loads pages: raw URLs and HTTP requests, drawing to a canvas, formatting text with word wrapping and line spacing. Part two views documents: constructing the HTML tree, block and inline layout, parsing and applying CSS, handling buttons and links. Part three runs applications: form submission, running interactive scripts that change the DOM, and the security trio of cookies, XSS and CSRF. Part four goes modern: visual effects and compositing, the event loop and rendering pipeline, GPU animations, the accessibility tree, images and iframes, and invalidation - reusing previous computation instead of redoing everything. It needs nothing but Python and your machine - no accounts, no paid tools - and it's been translated into Korean and Japanese with a discussion forum on GitHub. The exercise: tonight, do the first chapter - open a socket, send an HTTP request, parse the response and print the page body. That single evening demystifies more of the web than a semester of using frameworks, and the book's exercises let you stop after any part with something that works.
ptrs: Free online book: build a basic but complete browser in ~a couple thousand lines of Python, from networking to JavaScript
Part 1: HTTP requests, drawing to a canvas, text wrapping; Part 2: HTML tree, layout, CSS, links and buttons
Part 3: forms, interactive scripts, cookies, XSS and CSRF; Part 4: compositing, event loop, GPU animation, accessibility, invalidation
Runs on any machine with Python - no accounts, no cost, no special hardware
Tonight's exercise: chapter 1 - open a socket, request a page over HTTP, print its body
Back on the HN front page today; translations in Korean and Japanese, GitHub discussion forum
items.why: Bro, you USE a browser ten hours a day and your whole creator life runs on one - and right now it's magic to you. One weekend with this book and HTTP, CSS, cookies and rendering stop being magic and start being machinery you can exploit. That's a genuine edge for every site, tool and agent you build next. It costs nothing and runs on your PC as-is. This is the most legendary homework you'll ever assign yourself.
items.example: Chapter 1 has you write a small Python function that opens a TCP socket to a website, sends 'GET / HTTP/1.1' with a Host header, reads the response, splits off the headers, and prints the HTML body. In about an hour you've done by hand what every browser does a billion times a day - and the rest of the book keeps growing that same program.

questions.q: What do you build in Web Browser Engineering, and in what language?
questions.a: A basic but complete web browser, in Python - from networking through JavaScript.

questions.q: Name any three topics the book covers.
questions.a: Any three of: HTTP requests, HTML parsing, layout, CSS, forms, JavaScript/DOM, cookies/XSS/CSRF, compositing, the event loop, accessibility, invalidation.

questions.q: What do you need to start?
questions.a: Just Python on your machine - the book is free online and needs no accounts or extra hardware.

It starts with fetching a page from the internet and ends with animations and security. Each chapter leaves you with something that actually runs.

items.headline: Let Your Agent Drive the Browser You're Already Logged Into
items.deck: OpenCode Browse is a free, open-source MCP server plus a Chromium extension that hands your coding agent your real browser - your tabs, your logins, your extensions - with a polite handoff whenever it's your turn to type a password.
items.lead: OpenCode Browse, trending on Hacker News today, is a free open-source tool that lets your coding agent use your actual browser instead of a rented cloud one. It pairs an MCP server with a Chromium extension, so agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Zed can read pages, click, type and take screenshots using the sessions you are already signed into.
items.body: OpenCode Browse, trending on Hacker News today, is a free open-source tool that lets your coding agent use your actual browser instead of a rented cloud one. It pairs an MCP server with a Chromium extension, so agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or Zed can read pages, click, type and take screenshots using the sessions you are already signed into. The mechanics are considerate: agent tabs open in the background, grouped and collapsed out of your way. When the agent hits a moment that needs you - a login form, a 2FA prompt, a payment - it pauses, hands the tab back, and continues once you click Continue. You can also lend it a tab you already have open via the toolbar button, and restrict it to an allowed-sites list so it stays where you put it. It works with Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Helium, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium, installs from the Chrome Web Store with the extension walking you through setup, and has a PowerShell install line for Windows. Because it is any-MCP-client compatible, it plugs into whatever agent you already run. The comparison worth naming is Browserbase, the paid cloud-browser platform for agents: its free tier includes just 1 browser hour a month, the Developer plan is $20/month for 100 hours then $0.12 per hour, and Startup is $99/month. OpenCode Browse costs nothing and has no hour meter because the browser is yours. The tradeoff is real though: cloud browsers run while your machine is off and keep your accounts isolated, while Browse needs your browser open and shares your logged-in sessions - which is exactly why the allowed-sites list matters. The source is public at github.com/anomalyco/browse.
ptrs: Two parts: an MCP server plus a Chromium extension - agents read pages, click, type, screenshot and even record tabs
Agent tabs open in the background in collapsed groups, so it works alongside you instead of taking over your screen
Handoffs: the agent pauses at logins, 2FA prompts and payments, you do that step yourself, then click Continue
Lend a tab: the toolbar button hands the agent a tab you already have open; an allowed-sites list keeps it on the sites you name

Works with any MCP client (OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Zed) and with Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Helium, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium; Windows installs via irm https://opencode.ai/browse/install.ps1 | iex

Paid comparison: Browserbase's free tier is 1 browser hour/month, Developer is $20/month for 100 hours then $0.12/hour, Startup $99/month - Browse is free and unmetered, but needs your browser running and shares your logins
items.why: Bro, this is the missing piece between your agent experiments and the real internet. Every cool demo you have seen - agent fills a form, agent checks a price, agent posts a reel - needs a browser with logins, and the cloud ones charge you by the hour for a browser that knows nothing about you. This runs on your Windows PC today, no hardware upgrade, no API bill. Suit up your agent and let it fetch you a coffee-table's worth of research while you watch.
items.example: You ask your agent to check whether a design tool you use has a student discount. Instead of a sandboxed cloud browser hitting a login wall, Browse opens a background tab in your own Chrome where you're already signed in, reads the pricing page, screenshots the student tier, and hands the tab to you only if a payment or login step appears - you click Continue and it finishes the job.

questions.q: What are the two parts of OpenCode Browse?
questions.a: An MCP server and a Chromium browser extension.

questions.q: What happens when the agent reaches a login or payment step?
questions.a: It pauses and hands the tab back to you; you complete the step and click Continue.

questions.q: How does its cost compare to Browserbase?
questions.a: Browse is free and unmetered (your own browser); Browserbase's free tier is 1 browser hour/month and paid plans start at $20/month.

items.plain: AI agents can click around websites for you, but usually they use a rented browser on someone else's computer that isn't logged into anything - and you pay for every hour. This free tool lets the agent borrow YOUR browser, with your logins, like lending a friend your phone for one call. If it needs your password or card, it hands the phone back to you first.

items.headline: The Squircle: Why Your Phone's Icons Feel Softer Than a Rounded Square
items.deck: A squircle is the curve family between circle and square - and the reason iOS icons look smooth instead of clipped. The math just landed in CSS itself, so you can ship one with two lines of code.
items.lead: A squircle is a shape between a square and a circle, and there is no single definition - it is a family of parametrized curves. The Linebender wiki's squircle page, on Hacker News today, traces the whole family from Piet Hein's superellipse to Apple's iOS 7 icon shape to the brand-new CSS corner-shape property.
items.body: A squircle is a shape between a square and a circle, and there is no single definition - it is a family of parametrized curves. The Linebender wiki's squircle page, on Hacker News today, traces the whole family from Piet Hein's superellipse to Apple's iOS 7 icon shape to the brand-new CSS corner-shape property. The best-known squircle is the superellipse, |x|^n + |y|^n = 1: at n=2 you get a circle, and it approaches a square as n grows; Piet Hein popularized it and Martin Gardner told its story in Scientific American in 1977. There are two construction approaches: one continuous analytic curve, or straight flat sides joined to smooth corners - the second adapts to any rectangle without distorting the corner. When Apple switched icons from a rounded rectangle to a squircle in iOS 7 in 2013, early analysis guessed a superellipse of exponent 5, but extracting the actual Bezier curves showed it was a flat-sided squircle - and a slightly flawed one, with an extra straight segment and a touch of asymmetry. Figma's influential 'Desperately Seeking Squircles' post produced its own three-Bezier approximation. The quality test is continuity: a plain rounded rectangle has a kink where the arc meets the straight edge, while a good squircle has G2 continuity, meaning curvature changes smoothly - only clothoid squircles and superellipses with n above 2 achieve it. The practical news: squircles are now standardized in CSS via the corner-shape property in the box decorations spec, and Chromium implements a close two-Bezier-per-quadrant approximation. An Apple-like icon shape today is: aspect-ratio: 1; border-radius: 46.2%; corner-shape: superellipse(1.585) - the parameter being log2 of the superellipse exponent 3. The wiki also defines a handy 'gauge' measurement - the midpoint coordinate 0.5^(1/n) - for comparing squircles across variants.
ptrs: Superellipse: |x|^n + |y|^n = 1 - circle at n=2, approaches a square as n grows; popularized by Piet Hein, narrated by Martin Gardner in 1977
Two ways to build one: a single analytic curve, or flat sides plus smooth corners - the second keeps corners consistent across any aspect ratio
Apple moved icons to a squircle in iOS 7 (2013); the famous 'exponent 5 superellipse' guess was wrong - it's flat-sided, with tiny flaws (one extra straight segment, slight asymmetry)
The quality bar is G2 continuity - curvature easing smoothly with no kink; plain rounded rectangles fail it, clothoid and n>2 superellipse squircles pass
Squircles are now in CSS: corner-shape: superellipse(1.585) with border-radius: 46.2% approximates the Apple icon shape; Chromium uses a two-Bezier-per-quadrant approximation
'Gauge' = the midpoint coordinate 0.5^(1/n), a common ruler for comparing different squircle families
items.why: Legendary detail, bro: the difference between 'nice app icon' and 'why does this look cheap' is literally a curvature kink your eye catches in a millisecond. You are building interfaces and design taste is your moat - knowing WHY Apple's corner feels soft (G2 continuity, not magic) is the kind of knowledge that separates a designer from a template user. And it is two lines of CSS now. Challenge accepted?
items.example: You are styling a card component for a project. border-radius: 24px gives corners that visibly snap from straight edge to arc. Switching to corner-shape: superellipse(1.585) with a matched radius eases the curvature from zero at the flat side into the corner - the same continuous-curvature trick behind the iOS icon shape - and the card instantly reads as more polished.

questions.q: What is a superellipse's formula and what does n=2 give?
questions.a: |x|^n + |y|^n = 1; at n=2 it is a circle, approaching a square as n grows.

questions.q: Why does a plain rounded rectangle look less smooth than a squircle?
questions.a: Its arc meets the straight edge with a curvature kink; a good squircle has G2 continuity, so curvature changes smoothly.

questions.q: How do you get an Apple-like icon shape in CSS today?

items.plain: A rounded square is a square with its corners sawn off and replaced by circle arcs - look closely and there's a tiny bump where the straight part meets the curve. items.headline: Michael Mann vs Michael Mann: The 50-Year Paper Trail Behind Heat
items.deck: New Regency just sued Michael Mann to kill his copyright termination notices on Heat - and the whole fight turns on whether his 1980s drafts were written by the man or by the corporation that employs him.
items.lead: New Regency sued Michael Mann in Los Angeles federal court on November 13, asking a judge to declare his three copyright termination notices on Heat invalid. As Copyright Lately's breakdown explains, the case turns on a Hollywood structure every creator should understand: the loan-out company, and the question of who actually 'wrote' a screenplay - the person or his own corporation.
items.body: New Regency sued Michael Mann in Los Angeles federal court on November 13, asking a judge to declare his three copyright termination notices on Heat invalid. As Copyright Lately's breakdown explains, the case turns on a Hollywood structure every creator should understand: the loan-out company, and the question of who actually 'wrote' a screenplay - the person or his own corporation. The background rule is Section 203(a) of the Copyright Act: authors can terminate copyright grants roughly 35 years after making them - a second bite at the apple once a work proves valuable - but works made for hire are exempt, because the employer is legally the author. Hollywood talent routinely works through loan-out corporations they own, which formally employ them; if Mann wrote Heat as his loan-out's employee, nobody can terminate, because the company is the author and he is not. Mann's argument is narrower and more interesting than claiming his company was a sham: he says he wrote the early Heat drafts between 1981 and 1985 on his own, as what the studio calls 'an unemployed author.' The paper trail fights him: a 1976 loan-out deal with Columbia, a 1989 L.A. Takedown contract reciting he wrote as 'an employee-for-hire,' and the 1994 Warner Bros. sale of the Heat screenplay as a work made for hire - which Mann signed twice, and whose Copyright Office registration lists the author as 'Michael Mann Company, Inc.' His termination notices target an oral October 1988 agreement with two companies he controlled - no writing exists, and New Regency says his account of it changed when pressed - plus a written 1989 assignment to another Mann company, Ajar. The stakes are live: Heat 2 starts shooting January 19 with Amazon MGM's United Artists, Leonardo DiCaprio and Christian Bale, after Warner Bros. balked at a $170 million budget - and Amazon bought sequel rights twice, once from Mann personally and once from New Regency, hedging the dispute. Timing is everything: terminating the 1994 deal couldn't happen before 2030, while a 1988 grant gets Mann to 2028 - and even a win may not return the rights, since an oral grant transfers at most a nonexclusive license while New Regency's exclusive rights trace to the written 1994 deal. The 1995 film itself is safe either way under the derivative works exception, and legal precedent cuts both ways: Marvel v. Simon held that calling a work 'made for hire' after the fact doesn't make it one, while the Martha Graham case ruled the opposite for work created on the job. Most termination fights settle.
ptrs: Section 203(a): authors can terminate copyright grants ~35 years later; works made for hire are exempt - the employer is the legal author
The loan-out trap: write as your own corporation's employee and nobody can terminate - the company is the author, you are not
Mann's claim: he wrote the early Heat drafts personally in 1981-85, outside the loan-out - New Regency calls it an 'oral agreement with himself' it says he forgot for four decades
The paper trail: 1976 Columbia loan-out deal, 1989 'employee-for-hire' L.A. Takedown, 1994 Warner sale signed twice with the copyright registered to 'Michael Mann Company, Inc.'
Stakes: Heat 2 shoots January 19 with DiCaprio and Bale at Amazon MGM; Amazon bought sequel rights from BOTH sides; a 1988 grant terminates in 2028 vs 2030 for the written 1994 deal
Even winning may not return the rights - an oral grant conveys at most a nonexclusive license, and the studio's exclusive chain runs through the signed 1994 contract
items.why: You are building a creator business, so tattoo this on your brain: the contract structure around your work can matter more than the work. Termination rights are the law's way of giving creators a second payday 35 years on - and one 'work for hire' checkbox, signed casually, erases it. Mann made Heat and might still not own Heat. When your agency idea takes off, bro, you will remember this story every time someone hands you paperwork.
items.example: Imagine you write a script tonight, then next year form a company and 'sell' it the script in an email nobody saves. Decades later you try to reclaim the rights - but the studio's file shows every contract calling you an employee-for-hire, and your early deal has no paper. Mann's fight is exactly that scenario at blockbuster scale: the drafts, the dates and the signatures decide everything, not memory.

questions.q: What does Section 203(a) give authors?
questions.a: The right to terminate copyright grants roughly 35 years after making them - unless the work was made for hire.

questions.q: Why is Mann's loan-out company a problem for his termination claim?
questions.a: If he wrote Heat as his company's employee, the company is the legal author - companies can't terminate, and he wouldn't be the author.

questions.q: Why might winning the termination fight still not get Mann the rights?
questions.a: An oral grant transfers at most a nonexclusive license; New Regency's exclusive rights trace through the written 1994 deal.

items.plain: US law lets creators take back rights they sold after about 35 years - but not if the work was 'made for hire,' because then the employer owns it from day one. Michael Mann wrote Heat while working through a company he himself owned, so the studio says his company - not Michael Mann - was the author. He's basically arguing 'that wasn't me, that was my company,' which is hard when you signed papers for both.

items.headline: Windows 11 Is Tallying Which Coding Agents You Run
items.deck: A reverse engineer found a Windows component that watches for codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe and cursor.exe, records which ones you use as bits in a report, and queues it for upload unless you opted out of optional diagnostics.
items.lead: Security researcher Xusheng Li reverse-engineered a Windows 11 component, MissionControlAggregator.dll, and found it records which coding agents and developer tools you run - and uploads that list to Microsoft if optional diagnostic data is on, which it is by default in the US setup he tested. The post hit the Hacker News front page today.
items.body: Security researcher Xusheng Li reverse-engineered a Windows 11 component, MissionControlAggregator.dll, and found it records which coding agents and developer tools you run - and uploads that list to Microsoft if optional diagnostic data is on, which it is by default in the US setup he tested. The post hit the Hacker News front page today. The DLL contains explicit executable-name matchers: four CLI coding-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe and agy.exe, five desktop-agent slots for github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe and antigravity.exe, plus twelve broader developer-tool categories covering node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, code.exe and more - some verified by publisher (Node.js Foundation, Python Software Foundation, Microsoft). The feature flag is literally named CLICodingAgentUsage. The component does not scan your processes itself; it subscribes to existing Windows diagnostic events and notes matches. What it records is a bitmap - which tools were observed in a reporting window, not your prompts, code, or usage duration. Li confirmed the pipeline end to end on a live VM: renaming a copy of cmd.exe to codex.exe was enough to set the Codex bit, and the resulting Segments.SubCohorts report was found in DiagTrack's upload queue, marked optional diagnostic data. Because optional diagnostics default to on in the US installation he tested, most users who never changed privacy settings would be uploading it; the kill switch is Settings, Privacy & security, Diagnostics & feedback, 'Send optional diagnostic data' off. Two honest caveats from the post itself: a clean public-ISO install had the feature disabled by image default, so it is not proven active on every machine, and the report contains bits about tool names only - no prompt text or source code was found. Still, which AI agents and dev tools you run is itself revealing telemetry, and the HN discussion zeroed in on the default-on setting and the executable-name list hiding in a system DLL.
ptrs: MissionControlAggregator.dll embeds name matchers for codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, cursor.exe, agy.exe, antigravity.exe and more, behind a feature flag named CLICodingAgentUsage
Scope: 4 CLI coding-agent slots, 5 desktop-agent slots, 12 developer-tool categories (node, python, dotnet, gcc, clang, gdb, javac, devenv, code...), some publisher-verified
It records a bitmap of which tools were observed per reporting window - no prompts, no code, no usage duration, per the reverse engineering
Proven live: renaming cmd.exe to codex.exe set the Codex bit, and the report appeared in DiagTrack's upload queue as optional diagnostic data
Optional diagnostics are on by default in the US setup tested; turn off 'Send optional diagnostic data' under Settings > Privacy & security > Diagnostics & feedback
Caveats: a clean public-ISO VM had the feature off by default, so coverage across all Windows installs is unproven
items.why: Bro, you literally run coding agents on a Windows PC - this is about YOUR machine. Whether or not you mind Microsoft knowing you use Claude Code, the lesson is bigger: operating systems watch executable names, and 'optional' telemetry defaults matter. Two-minute check tonight: Settings, Diagnostics & feedback, and make an informed choice instead of a default one. That is the difference between a user and a power user. Suit up.
items.example: You install Codex CLI and run it for an afternoon. Windows' app-usage events note a process named codex.exe; the aggregator's matcher sets the 'Codex CLI' bit in its saved state; at the next reporting boundary that bit goes into a Segments.SubCohorts event, which - with optional diagnostics enabled - sits in DiagTrack's upload queue to Microsoft. Flip the diagnostics toggle off and the queue stops accepting it.

questions.q: What does the Windows component record about coding agents?
questions.a: A bitmap of which agent and tool executables were observed in a reporting window - not prompts, code or duration.

questions.q: How did the researcher prove detection works?
questions.a: He renamed a copy of cmd.exe to codex.exe and the Codex slot lit up - the executable name alone triggers it.

questions.q: How do you stop the upload?
questions.a: Settings > Privacy & security > Diagnostics & feedback, turn off 'Send optional diagnostic data'.

items.plain: Windows keeps a checklist of which programmer tools and AI coding assistants you open, like a hall monitor noting who enters the library. It doesn't read your code or prompts - just the program names. That list gets sent to Microsoft unless you switch off 'optional diagnostic data' in privacy settings, which takes about a minute.

items.headline: RoPE: Spin the Vectors, Keep the Distance
items.deck: Sebastian Raschka's new walkthrough explains how modern LLMs know word order: instead of adding position numbers to tokens, RoPE rotates each token's query and key arrows inside attention - so what matters is how far apart two words are, not where they sit.
items.lead: In a new deep-dive, Sebastian Raschka traces how LLMs encode token order, from GPT-2's learned position vectors to RoPE, the method inside most 2026 open-weight models. RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding, from Su et al.'s 2021 RoFormer paper) rotates each token's query and key vectors inside attention by an angle proportional to its position - and because only the difference between two rotations survives in the dot product, the attention score depends on how far apart two tokens are, not their absolute seats.
items.body: In a new deep-dive, Sebastian Raschka traces how LLMs encode token order, from GPT-2's learned position vectors to RoPE, the method inside most 2026 open-weight models. RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding, from Su et al.'s 2021 RoFormer paper) rotates each token's query and key vectors inside attention by an angle proportional to its position - and because only the difference between two rotations survives in the dot product, the attention score depends on how far apart two tokens are, not their absolute seats. Order matters because 'the red fox jumps over the gray fox' and 'the gray fox jumps over the red fox' share every token but not their meaning. GPT-2 handled this with a learned table of 1,024 position vectors added to token embeddings - workable, but the table caps context length before training and scales terribly: in GPT-2 Medium those vectors are 0.30% of weights at 1,024 positions, yet would exceed 22% at a 100k context. The original 2017 transformer used fixed sine/cosine position vectors instead - still absolute. RoPE moves the idea inside attention: query and key features are split into pairs, and each pair rotates as a little arrow by an angle equal to the token position times that pair's frequency (frequencies follow theta_i = base^(-2i/d) with base 10,000, so a d=8 head gets 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 radians per position). Rotation preserves arrow length; what changes is the angle between two tokens' arrows. His worked example: identical starting pairs score 26 unrotated and 13 after position rotation - exactly 26 x cos(60 degrees) for tokens three positions apart at 20 degrees per position. Shift both tokens by the same amount (say, a 100-token system prompt) and both arrows gain the same extra spin, so their angle - and score - is unchanged. Value vectors bypass rotation entirely. Recent models like MiniMax-M3 apply RoPE inside every attention block, and variants like partial RoPE rotate only part of each head.
ptrs: Why positions at all: 'the red fox jumps over the gray fox' and its swapped twin share every token but not their meaning, so the model must know who sits where.

GPT-2's way: a learned table of 1,024 position vectors added to token embeddings - but the table caps context length before training, and in GPT-2 Medium it is 0.30% of weights at 1,024 positions yet would exceed 22% at 100k context. The 2017 transformer's fixed sine/cosine vectors were still absolute too.

RoPE's way: query and key features split into pairs, each pair rotates like a tiny arrow by position x frequency; frequencies follow theta_i = base^(-2i/d) with base 10,000, so a d=8 head spins its four pairs at 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 radians per position. Value vectors skip the spin.

The payoff: rotation preserves arrow length, so the dot product becomes length x length x cos(angle between) - and that angle depends only on the offset between tokens. His worked example: identical pairs score 26 unrotated and exactly 13 (= 26 x cos 60 degrees) when three positions apart at 20 degrees per position.

Prefix-proof: add a 100-token system prompt and both arrows gain the same extra rotation, so their relative score survives; that is the property absolute methods lack. Recent models like MiniMax-M3 apply RoPE inside every attention block, and partial-RoPE variants rotate only part of each head.
items.why: This is the single most exam-able, interview-able building block in your syllabus, and bro, most students memorize 'RoPE good' without knowing WHY. You now know the actual mechanic: spin arrows, keep the angle. When your professor asks why long contexts don't break relative meaning, you'll answer with cosines while everyone else checks their notes. Legendary.
items.example: Concrete intuition to steal: a system prompt of any length is just a shared shift - in RoPE land it rotates every token's arrows by the same extra amount, so 'fox' three seats away from 'the' still scores exactly as strongly (his example holds at 13 whether the pair sits at positions 2 and 5 or 102 and 105). That is why chat models can carry long system prompts without scrambling sentence geometry.

questions.q: What does RoPE rotate, and where?
questions.a: Each token's query and key vectors, inside the attention blocks; value vectors are not rotated.

questions.q: Why does a shared position shift (like a long system prompt) preserve attention scores under RoPE?
questions.a: Both vectors gain the same extra rotation, so the angle between them - and their dot product - stays the same.

questions.q: What capped GPT-2's context length?
questions.a: Its learned table of 1,024 position vectors, fixed before training; growing it to 100k positions would cost over 22% of the model's weights.

items.plain: Imagine every word in a sentence holding a little compass needle. RoPE turns each needle clockwise by how far the word is from the start - word 5 turns more than word 2. When two words 'look' at each other, only the difference in their needle angles matters, so moving the whole sentence somewhere else changes nothing between them. That's how the model tracks word order without writing down seat numbers.

items.headline: The Empty Space Is the Second Logo
items.deck: Negative space turns the background of a mark into a hidden picture - the FedEx-style 'aha' that makes people look twice. A complete guide breaks down the principles, the five techniques and a six-step process to build your own.
items.lead: Logo.app's complete guide to negative space logos argues the strongest marks carry two pictures: the one you draw (positive space) and the one hiding in the gaps you left (negative space). Done well, the hidden layer adds meaning with zero extra clutter - and the article lays out the principles, five concrete techniques and a step-by-step process to design one.
items.body: Logo.app's complete guide to negative space logos argues the strongest marks carry two pictures: the one you draw (positive space) and the one hiding in the gaps you left (negative space). Done well, the hidden layer adds meaning with zero extra clutter - and the article lays out the principles, five concrete techniques and a step-by-step process to design one. The psychology is figure-ground perception (the Rubin's vase illusion): your brain decides what's figure and what's background, and shaping the background on purpose creates an 'aha' moment that makes brands stick. There's a key distinction between decorative gaps (look nice) and conceptual gaps (carry meaning). The classics prove it: Amazon's arrow runs A to Z and doubles as a smile; Formula 1 hides a '1' between the F and the speed stripes; Toyota's three ovals contain every letter of 'Toyota'; the WWF panda's white areas complete its body; Toblerone's mountain hides a bear for Bern, the City of Bears; the Guild of Food Writers merges a fountain pen nib and a spoon into one outline. The principles: simplicity first (the main shape must read even if nobody spots the trick), high contrast, pass the silhouette test in solid black, design in one color before adding any, and make gaps feel deliberate rather than accidental. The process: pick two concepts to fuse (literal + metaphorical), choose wordmark or symbol, sketch broad shapes, hunt overlaps and natural gaps (between letters, inside loops, between limbs), refine and test with non-designers, then digitize in vector tools - Illustrator, Figma, Affinity or free Inkscape. Five techniques to find the hidden shape: subtraction (carve it out), overlapping outlines that share an edge, letterform sculpting, geometric construction, and shadow-and-light tricks. Finish with the checklist: strangers should name both images within three seconds, it must survive favicon size, monochrome, reversed colors and textured backgrounds, plus a cultural check on the hidden symbol.
ptrs: The psychology: figure-ground perception (Rubin's vase) - your brain picks a figure and a ground, and shaping the ground on purpose creates an 'aha' moment that makes the brand stick. Distinguish decorative gaps (pretty) from conceptual gaps (meaningful).

The classics: Amazon's A-to-Z arrow doubles as a smile; Formula 1 hides a '1' between the F and the stripes; Toyota's three ovals contain every letter of 'Toyota'; the WWF panda's white completes its body; Toblerone's mountain hides Bern's bear; the Guild of Food Writers merges a pen nib and a spoon into one outline.

The principles: simplicity first (the mark must work even if nobody spots the trick), high contrast, pass the silhouette test in solid black, design in one color first, and every gap must feel deliberate.

The six steps: define two concepts to fuse (literal + metaphorical), pick wordmark or symbol, sketch broad shapes, hunt overlaps and natural gaps (between letters, inside loops, between limbs), refine and test with non-designers, digitize in vectors (Illustrator, Figma, Affinity, or free Inkscape).

Five techniques: subtraction (carve the shape out), overlapping outlines that share an edge, letterform sculpting, geometric construction, and shadow-and-light tricks. Checklist to finish: strangers name both images in 3 seconds, survives favicon size, monochrome and reversed, works on textured backgrounds, passes a cultural check.
items.why: Your TechBlast identity and future agency need a mark that works as a reel watermark at 60 pixels AND rewards a second look - that is exactly the negative-space brief. Two ideas, one shape, no clutter: 'video + blast', 'AI + art'. The aha moment is free memorability, bro - people who solve the puzzle feel smart and remember YOU for it.
items.example: Try the guide's own exercise tonight: pick a three-letter word (say 'art') and hide a related icon inside the letters using only solid black and white - then the second exercise: sketch ten animal silhouettes and fit a second object into the gaps between legs, wings and tails. Fifteen minutes per exercise, pen and paper, no software.

questions.q: What is the silhouette test?
questions.a: Reduce the logo to solid black on white - if the identity still reads, the shape is strong enough.

questions.q: Name two famous negative-space logos and their hidden elements.
questions.a: Formula 1 hides a '1' between the F and stripes; Toblerone's mountain hides a bear (Amazon's A-to-Z smile and the WWF panda also count).

questions.q: What is the difference between decorative and conceptual negative space?
questions.a: Decorative gaps just look good; conceptual gaps carry meaning, narrative or brand values.

items.plain: Look at a picture of two faces staring at each other and you might also see a vase between them - that vase is the 'empty' space doing a job. Logo designers shape that emptiness on purpose, so the gap inside a picture hides a second picture. It's like folding paper and cutting one hole that turns out to be a star.

items.headline: Hear the Future Before You See It
items.deck: The smoothest edits in film are the ones you never notice: J-cuts and L-cuts stagger picture and sound so scenes flow like real conversation. One guide breaks down split edits, match cuts and how to build them in any editor.
items.lead: DFI Rentals' editing guide unpacks the invisible machinery of scene flow: in a J-cut, the next shot's audio starts before its picture (you hear the future before you see it); in an L-cut, the previous shot's sound lingers over the new image. Together they're called split edits - and they're why well-edited dialogue feels alive instead of robotic.
items.body: DFI Rentals' editing guide unpacks the invisible machinery of scene flow: in a J-cut, the next shot's audio starts before its picture (you hear the future before you see it); in an L-cut, the previous shot's sound lingers over the new image. Together they're called split edits - and they're why well-edited dialogue feels alive instead of robotic. Cut a conversation with picture and sound snapping over together and it plays like a tennis match; real people react before the other finishes talking, so editors cut to a listener while the speaker's line trails on (L-cut) or let the next line begin over the current face (J-cut). The names are literal timeline shapes: on an NLE timeline the staggered audio and video blocks form a J or an L. A practical superpower: because sound and picture are decoupled, you can pair the best-framed take with the best-read take. Rules of thumb: J-cut to set up the next scene early or ease into a new location; L-cut to hold a reaction or let emotion bleed forward; keep overlaps subtle - a few frames to a second or two, and if the audience notices the stagger it's too long. The guide also covers the match cut, which links shots by shared shape, color or movement: Lawrence of Arabia's lit match to desert sunrise (editor Anne V. Coates; the film won the 1963 editing Oscar, and Spielberg has said that transition blew him away as a youth), 2001's bone to space station (editor Ray Lovejoy), and The Graduate's pool-to-bedroom drift. The rest of the vocabulary: cutting on action (movement hides the cut), jump cut (deliberate continuity break), cross-cut/parallel editing (The Godfather's baptism), cutaway (cover an edit), smash cut (jarring contrast). To build a split edit: lay both clips back to back, unlink audio from video, drag the incoming audio left (J) or extend the outgoing audio right (L), add short crossfades, and trim by frames. And the on-set truth: split edits live or die on coverage with handles and clean separated sound.
ptrs: J-cut: the next shot's audio starts before its picture - also called audio advance/lead/under; named for the J shape the staggered clips make on an NLE timeline. L-cut: the previous shot's sound trails over the new picture. Together: split edits.

Why they work: cutting picture-and-sound together feels like a robotic tennis match; real conversation reacts before lines finish, so trail the speaker's audio over the listener (L) or start the next line over the current face (J).
Superpower: decoupled tracks let you pair the best-framed take with the best-read take. Keep overlaps subtle - a few frames to a second or two; if the audience notices the stagger, it's too long.

Match cuts link shots by shared shape, color or movement: Lawrence of Arabia's match-flame to desert sunrise (editor Anne V. Coates; 1963 editing Oscar; Spielberg says it blew him away), 2001's bone to space station (editor Ray Lovejoy), The Graduate's pool-to-bedroom drift.

Vocabulary worth keeping: cutting on action (movement hides the cut), jump cut (deliberate break), cross-cut/parallel editing (The Godfather's baptism), cutaway, smash cut. To build one: unlink audio and video, drag the incoming audio left (J) or extend the outgoing right (L), add short crossfades, trim by frames - and shoot coverage with handles plus clean sound, because split edits are really audio edits.
items.why: Your reels are 90% dialogue and reaction - this is the single cheapest upgrade to how professional they feel. Right now you probably cut picture-and-sound together, which is exactly the tennis-match stiffness this guide kills. One staggered audio drag in Premiere or Resolve and your next two-person skit breathes like TV. Suit up your timeline.
items.example: Next reel with a friend: when they start their punchline, let their audio begin half a second BEFORE the picture cuts to them (J-cut) - the audience leans in. Then hold THEIR reaction face while your reply's audio starts over it (L-cut). Two drags, zero new footage, instantly less robotic.

questions.q: What is a J-cut?
questions.a: The next shot's audio starts playing before its picture appears - you hear the future before you see it.

questions.q: What is an L-cut used for?
questions.a: Lingering on a reaction or letting the previous scene's emotion bleed into the next shot.

questions.q: How long should the audio overlap be?
questions.a: Subtle - a few frames to a second or two; if the audience notices the stagger, it's too long.

items.plain: In real life, you often hear something before you turn to look at it - a friend laughs before you see their face. Editors copy that: they let the sound from the next moment slip in a little early, or let the current sound hang on a little late, instead of switching picture and sound at the same instant. That's why movie conversations feel smooth instead of choppy.

items.headline: Your Old Short Links Are Up for Grabs
items.deck: A Bitly flaw let strangers re-register old, inactive short links and point them anywhere - a 2011 Burger King tweet suddenly led to a list of Nazi camps, and a sample of 97 old links shows 7 already hijacked.
items.lead: Ransomnews found that old Bitly short links are being re-registered by strangers and redirected: a 2011 Burger King tweet about a restaurant locator suddenly pointed at Wikipedia's list of Nazi concentration camps, and a McDonald's tweet from the same year led to an article about the September 11 attacks. Nobody's account was hacked - the links changed hands on Bitly's side, and Bitly has now confirmed the issue.
items.body: Ransomnews found that old Bitly short links are being re-registered by strangers and redirected: a 2011 Burger King tweet about a restaurant locator suddenly pointed at Wikipedia's list of Nazi concentration camps, and a McDonald's tweet from the same year led to an article about the September 11 attacks. Nobody's account was hacked - the links changed hands on Bitly's side, and Bitly has now confirmed the issue. The Burger King link (posted 24 July 2011) shows a creation time of 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 on Bitly's public info page; the McDonald's link was re-created 18 minutes earlier. A post quoting the Burger King tweet passed 2 million views within hours, and both original tweets later became unavailable. Checking 97 Bitly links in Donald Trump's tweets from 2009-2013, Ransomnews found 40 still original, 49 re-created later but still leading where the tweets suggest (48 of them in a single 17-minute run on 26 May 2023), 7 leading somewhere else - four registered on 15 November alone, opening a Roblox profile, two YouTube videos and a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein - and 1 blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam. Bitly's own help pages say a bit.ly ending cannot be reused even after the account behind it is deleted, and a similar bug was reportedly fixed in February 2025. You can audit any short link by adding a '+' to its address to see its destination and creation date. Bitly confirmed on X at 19:13 UTC that 'bad actors' repurposed 'certain old, inactive links', said it suspended the accounts involved and is disabling affected links; by 19:22 UTC the brand links showed 'Link Deactivated'. CNN reported old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the US Department of Defense were also affected (Ransomnews did not independently check those). The story sat at 170+ points on Hacker News, where commenters discussed link rot and whether platforms should freeze legacy short links - community reaction, not established fact.
ptrs: The Burger King link (posted 24 July 2011) shows a creation time of 05:32 UTC on 15 November 2026 on Bitly's public info page; the McDonald's link was re-created 18 minutes earlier, at 05:14 UTC. A quoting post passed 2 million views within hours; both original tweets later became unavailable.

The 97-link sample (Trump tweets 2009-2013): 40 still original, 49 re-created later but still leading where the tweets suggest (48 in a single 17-minute run on 26 May 2023), 7 leading somewhere else, 1 blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam.
The four hijacked on 15 November (registered 07:49-09:57 UTC) opened a Roblox profile, two YouTube videos and a Wikipedia article about Trump and Jeffrey Epstein.

Bitly's own help pages say a bit.ly ending cannot be reused even after the account behind it is deleted; a similar bug was reportedly fixed in February 2025. Audit any short link yourself: add '+' to its address to see destination and creation date.

Bitly confirmed on X at 19:13 UTC that 'bad actors' repurposed 'certain old, inactive links', suspended the accounts and is disabling affected links; by 19:22 UTC the brand links showed 'Link Deactivated'. CNN reported old posts from Bill Gates, Justin Trudeau, Mike Pence, the FBI and the DoD were affected too (not independently checked by Ransomnews).
HN discussion (170+ points): commenters discussed link rot and whether platforms should freeze legacy short links - community reaction, not established fact.
items.why: Every link you drop in your reel bios and video descriptions is an asset with an expiry date you don't control, bro. If you ever switch shorteners or let an account lapse, this is the failure mode: someone re-registers the slug and your old content points wherever they want. Owning your own domain for redirects isn't paranoia - it's brand insurance.
items.example: Audit habit from the article itself: take any bit.ly link you've ever posted, add '+' to the end, and read the destination and creation date. If the creation date is years newer than the post it sits in, the link changed hands - exactly how researchers confirmed the 2011 tweets were carrying 2026 links.

questions.q: Were Burger King's or McDonald's accounts hacked?
questions.a: No - the old Bitly links inside their tweets were re-registered by someone else; nothing was posted from either account.

questions.q: In the 97-link sample, how many led somewhere unintended?
questions.a: 7 led somewhere else and 1 was blocked by Bitly; 40 were still original and 49 re-created but still correct.

questions.q: How can you check where a bit.ly link really goes?
questions.a: Add a '+' to the end of the address to see Bitly's public info page with its destination and creation date.

items.plain: A short link is like a mailbox number at a post office. The post office promised your number stays yours forever - but a bug let other people rent old, abandoned mailbox numbers and stuff them with their own mail. Letters (and tweets) that point to those boxes now deliver something their owners never chose.

items.headline: Claude Fixed a Jeep Older Than Its Driver's Tools
items.deck: A creator wired a $3 Arduino into his 1994 Jeep's pre-OBD2 computer and let Claude Code and Codex diagnose it, read its fuel tables, and run their own code inside the ECU - until the car finally passed California smog.
items.lead: In a viral build log, Muhammad Zulali shows how he used Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex to talk to his 1994 Jeep Cherokee's computer - a machine so old it predates the OBD2 port, with no official tool worth finding. Over about a week, the agents read live sensor data through a $3 Arduino Nano, uncovered a California-specific fuel quirk, and eventually ran their own code inside the ECU - and the Jeep passed its smog test.
items.body: In a viral build log, Muhammad Zulali shows how he used Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex to talk to his 1994 Jeep Cherokee's computer - a machine so old it predates the OBD2 port, with no official tool worth finding. Over about a week, the agents read live sensor data through a $3 Arduino Nano, uncovered a California-specific fuel quirk, and eventually ran their own code inside the ECU - and the Jeep passed its smog test. The car was failing California smog at 25 mph with high NOx, and a new O2 sensor made the 15 mph reading explode from around 80 to 900 - at $100 per test, guessing parts wasn't sustainable. Claude Code identified the Jeep's old, slow SCI protocol and the backwards signal wire, and walked him through wiring a $3 Arduino Nano on a breadboard as a translator (about $15 total with jumpers); the first reading came at 1:30 AM after pulling resistors that drowned the signal. Logging drives with a MacBook on the passenger seat, the agents caught the computer reporting speed doubled, a fuel-trim reading that looked like +22% added fuel but turned out to be fuel REMOVED (the old Chrysler Scanner convention misled them), and a fuel rail at a terrible 10 PSI. Claude even primed the fuel pump for about 10 seconds - its first write action - before they realized the real culprit: his California-market ECU trims fuel down at exactly the loads the smog test uses, unlike federal cars, a difference of about a quarter percent of fuel. Reflashing to federal settings was impossible - his computer was built in December 1993, four months before these ECUs became programmable. So Codex found that the 1994 computer will simply RUN a tiny program sent over the same three wires, riding its main loop about 90 times a second; when the ECU's own code overwrote RAM after a few seconds, Codex put the program on the EEPROM instead. With the agents reading everything and adding their own code, the Jeep passed smog. He's posted the full wiring and code on GitHub, and ends the video asking: what else can you plug your agent into? The story drew 339+ points on Hacker News, where commenters traded their own pre-OBD stories and debated agents controlling physical machines - community reaction, not established fact.
ptrs: The problem: failing California smog at 25 mph with high NOx; a new O2 sensor made the 15 mph reading explode from ~80 to 900, and each smog retest costs about $100 - guessing parts was bleeding money.

The way in: Claude Code identified the Jeep's ancient SCI protocol and backwards signal wire; a $3 Arduino Nano on a breadboard (~$15 all-in) became the translator, with the first reading at 1:30 AM after pulling resistors that drowned the signal.

What the agents caught while logging drives: the ECU reporting speed doubled, a fuel-trim reading that looked like +22% added fuel but was actually fuel REMOVED (the old Chrysler Scanner convention misled them), and a fuel rail at 10 PSI; Claude also primed the fuel pump for ~10 seconds - its first write to the car.

The real culprit: his California-market ECU trims fuel down at exactly the loads the smog test uses, unlike federal cars (about a quarter percent of fuel). Reflashing was impossible - his computer was built December 1993, four months before these ECUs became programmable.

Codex's unlock: the 1994 computer runs tiny programs sent over the same three wires, riding its main loop ~90 times a second; when the ECU's own code overwrote RAM after a few seconds, Codex put the program on the EEPROM. The Jeep passed smog, and the full wiring and code are on GitHub.
HN discussion (339+ points): commenters traded their own pre-OBD2 stories and debated agents controlling physical machines - community reaction, not established fact.
items.why: This is the coding-agent story of the week for you specifically: not another SaaS demo, but agents debugging a PHYSICAL system older than the tools built for it. Notice the workflow - the human did the wiring and driving, the agents did protocol archaeology, logging analysis and memory work. That division of labor is the actual skill worth copying for any hardware project you touch.
items.example: Steal the pattern, not the car: point a coding agent at any obscure device protocol (an old printer, a treadmill, a scooter battery), let it identify the protocol and draft the wiring, then log real data before changing anything. The video's discipline - read-only first, weeks of logs, backups before the first write - is why it ended in a passed test instead of a bricked ECU.

questions.q: How did the agents talk to a car with no OBD2 port?
questions.a: Through the Jeep's old SCI protocol, translated by a $3 Arduino Nano on a breadboard wired to the diagnostic plug.

questions.q: Why couldn't the ECU just be reflashed?
questions.a: His computer was built in December 1993, about four months before these ECUs gained the physical parts for programming mode.

questions.q: What did Codex do that Claude hadn't?
questions.a: Got the 1994 computer to run their own program - first riding the main loop in RAM, then persisted on the EEPROM after RAM got overwritten.

items.plain: Old cars have small computers, but this one is so old there's no normal plug to read it. The owner built a tiny translator from a cheap chip, and an AI assistant learned the car's old language, listened to its sensors while driving, and figured out why it kept failing its emissions test - like using a translator app to interview a grandpa machine about its health.

items.headline: Host Your Own Google Maps for Pocket Change
items.deck: PMTiles packs an entire map into one file you can serve from cheap CDN storage - a Europe session costs about $0.00005 in bandwidth versus Mapbox's $5 per 1,000 map loads. Here's the whole setup.
items.lead: Bruce Röttgers' guide shows how Protomaps' PMTiles format makes self-hosting map tiles almost trivial: the whole map ships as one single file served over HTTP Range requests, so any CDN that can cache ranges can host it - no tile server, no database. His real numbers: storing the 139GB world map runs about $5/month, and loading a map of Europe plus zooming into a city transfers ~5MB, or $0.00005.
items.body: Bruce Röttgers' guide shows how Protomaps' PMTiles format makes self-hosting map tiles almost trivial: the whole map ships as one single file served over HTTP Range requests, so any CDN that can cache ranges can host it - no tile server, no database. His real numbers: storing the 139GB world map runs about $5/month, and loading a map of Europe plus zooming into a city transfers ~5MB, or $0.00005. The comparison that stings: Mapbox charges $5 per 1,000 map loads once you exhaust the free tier - at roughly $0.05 per 1,000 loads, self-hosting can be around 100x cheaper, though Mapbox's flat per-visit fee is at least predictable. The setup he documents: grab the daily world build from Protomaps' build page, or use the CLI to extract just your bounding box and zoom levels for a much smaller file; deploy to Bunny.net (it caches Range requests, is EU-based, and drops the last octet of IP addresses by default) using an S3-compatible storage zone and rclone (the HTTP API upload timed out for him at 15 minutes); then create a pull zone with 'Optimize for large object delivery' enabled so Range requests cache, restrict allowed CORS referrers so strangers can't embed your tiles, and add a 10kB/s speed limit after 10MB per request so nobody downloads the whole planet on your bill. Bandwidth costs $0.01/GB to Europe/North America ($0.005/GB on the Volume network); storage runs $0.01 to $0.055/GB/month depending on replication. Cloudflare works too but needs an edge function to translate x/y/z tile URLs into Range requests. Embedding is the standard MapLibre GL library plus the pmtiles npm package. The result: your own cost-effective, highly available map of the world (or just your city) that no pricing email can take away.
ptrs: PMTiles: a tile format that ships in a single file, read via HTTP Range requests - any CDN that caches ranges can host it, no tile server needed; Cloudflare works too but needs an edge function to translate x/y/z URLs into ranges.
Get maps: download the daily world build from Protomaps' build page (139GB), or use the CLI to extract only your bounding box and zoom levels for a much smaller file.

Real costs on Bunny.net: bandwidth $0.01/GB to Europe/North America ($0.005/GB on the Volume network); storage $0.01-0.055/GB/month by replication; the 139GB world map at 5x replication is about $5/month; loading Europe + zooming to a city is ~5MB = $0.00005.

The comparison: Mapbox charges $5 per 1,000 map loads after the free tier - self-hosting at roughly $0.05 per 1,000 loads can be ~100x cheaper, though Mapbox's flat per-visit fee is predictable regardless of user behavior.

Setup gotchas he hit: use an S3-compatible storage zone with rclone (the HTTP API upload timed out at 15 minutes); enable 'Optimize for large object delivery' so ranges cache; restrict CORS referrers; add a 10kB/s-after-10MB speed limit so nobody downloads the whole file on your bill. Embed with MapLibre GL + the pmtiles npm package.
items.why: Every travel vlog map animation, delivery tracker or 'stores near you' feature you've storyboarded pays the Google/Mapbox tax - this is the free-ish escape hatch. A city-sized extract costs you basically nothing to host, it's a legit weekend build for your portfolio, and 'self-hosted my own map stack' is a genuinely impressive line in an AIML resume. Challenge issued.
items.example: Weekend build: use the Protomaps CLI to extract just Ahmedabad's bounding box at city zoom levels (a tiny file instead of 139GB), push it to a Bunny storage zone with rclone, and embed it in a plain HTML page with MapLibre GL. Total running cost: cents per month - and every future project that needs a map is now free.

questions.q: What makes PMTiles easy to host?
questions.a: The whole map is one file read via HTTP Range requests, so any CDN that caches ranges can serve it - no tile server or database.

questions.q: What did the world map cost to store, and a Europe browsing session to serve?
questions.a: About $5/month to store the 139GB file (5x replication) and roughly $0.00005 for a ~5MB Europe session.

questions.q: Which two settings protect your CDN bill?
questions.a: Restricting allowed CORS referrers, and limiting download speed (10kB/s) after 10MB per request so nobody pulls the whole file.

items.plain: Map websites usually rent their maps by the visit, like paying a toll every time someone looks. PMTiles is like photocopying the entire atlas into one file you keep on a cheap shelf on the internet - visitors read pages straight from your copy, and the toll booth is out of the loop.

items.headline: Your Prompt's Language Sets Its Power Bill
items.deck: University of Michigan researchers metered the electricity LLMs burn per answer across 122 languages: Hindi cost 7.9x and Bengali 15.3x the energy of an equivalent English prompt - and 5.2 billion people's first language costs more than double.
items.lead: A University of Michigan team asked three open models - Alibaba's Qwen 3, Google's Gemma 3 and Meta's Llama 3.1 - the same reading-comprehension questions in 122 languages and metered the energy each answer used. Generating non-English text burned 1.4 to 180 times more energy than English, and the languages with the highest energy cost also tended to produce less accurate answers.
items.body: A University of Michigan team asked three open models - Alibaba's Qwen 3, Google's Gemma 3 and Meta's Llama 3.1 - the same reading-comprehension questions in 122 languages and metered the energy each answer used. Generating non-English text burned 1.4 to 180 times more energy than English, and the languages with the highest energy cost also tended to produce less accurate answers. Western European languages came in at roughly twice English's energy or less, and Spanish and Chinese sat around 2x even though each has more native speakers than English. Hindi needed 7.9x and Bengali 15.3x the energy of an equivalent English prompt; Urdu and several Indic languages - first languages for more than 800 million people combined - cost over 4x. The disparity is greatest in languages that don't use Latin script and have less digital training content. The team used the Belebele benchmark, measured joules with Michigan's ML.Energy framework, and cross-checked with grade-school math problems and open-ended prompts translated via Meta's No Language Left Behind. Adding demographic data from Ethnologue, they estimate about 5.2 billion people must spend more than twice the energy to generate text in their first language compared with English speakers. Their recommended fixes: route queries to models tailored to specific languages, translate prompts to English before a general model when the translation is reliable, and crowdsource native speakers to build training resources. The study was presented at EMNLP and funded in part by the NSF and DARPA.
ptrs: Western European languages came in at roughly twice English's energy or less; Spanish and Chinese sat around 2x even though each has more native speakers than English.
Hindi needed 7.9x and Bengali 15.3x the energy of an equivalent English prompt; Urdu and several Indic languages - first languages for over 800 million people combined - cost more than 4x.

The gap is worst in languages that don't use Latin script and have less digital training content; the study ran on the Belebele dataset (122 languages), measured joules with Michigan's ML.Energy framework, and cross-checked with math word problems and open-ended prompts translated using Meta's No Language Left Behind.

About 5.2 billion people must spend more than twice the energy to generate text in their first language compared with English speakers, per the researchers' measurements plus Ethnologue demographic data.

Recommended fixes: route queries to language-specific models, translate prompts to English first when translation is reliable, and crowdsource native speakers for training resources. Presented at EMNLP; funded partly by the NSF and DARPA.
items.why: Suit up, because this one is personal: you're an AIML student in India, and half your family group chat types in Hindi or Gujarati. When you build for Indian users, this double penalty - higher cost AND lower accuracy - is your design constraint, not a fun fact. An English-first pipeline is cheaper per answer today, but your users shouldn't have to switch languages to afford your app. Knowing that tokenizers charge more per word in non-Latin scripts is how you price, cache and route like a pro.
items.example: Concrete playbook from the study itself: if your app serves Hindi users, one suggested architecture translates the incoming prompt to English (when translation is reliable), runs the general model, and translates back - trading a small translation overhead for a big cut in generation energy, instead of letting one user cost 7.9x another for the same answer.

questions.q: How much more energy did Hindi prompts use than equivalent English ones?
questions.a: 7.9 times more; Bengali was 15.3 times more.

questions.q: Which three open models were metered?
questions.a: Alibaba's Qwen 3, Google's Gemma 3 and Meta's Llama 3.1.

questions.q: Name one fix the researchers recommend.
questions.a: Route queries to language-specific models - or translate prompts to English first when the translation is reliable.

items.plain: AI models chop text into little pieces called tokens before they think. Languages with less online training data get chopped into more pieces for the same sentence - like paying airline fees per suitcase and watching your one bag get split into fifteen. More pieces means more computing work, so the same question literally takes more electricity to answer in Hindi or Bengali than in English.
