items.headline: Grids: Decide Once, Then Stop Deciding
items.deck: A grid is not decoration - it is format, margins, leading, columns and fields decided once and held consistently. One step-by-step method walks from a blank A4 page to a full typographic grid in fifteen minutes.
items.lead: Design studio Fengo published a start-to-finish recipe for building a grid system: pick the format first, set margins (canon or deliberate), then let the body text's line height become the ruler for everything else. From that point on, columns, image blocks and headings all snap to the same invisible rhythm - which is why gridded work reads as one coherent whole.
items.body: Design studio Fengo published a start-to-finish recipe for building a grid system: pick the format first, set margins (canon or deliberate), then let the body text's line height become the ruler for everything else. From that point on, columns, image blocks and headings all snap to the same invisible rhythm - which is why gridded work reads as one coherent whole. Margins can come from a canon: the Van de Graaf construction divides the page into ninths - inner margin 1/9 of the width, outer 2/9, top 1/9 of the height, bottom 2/9 - giving the classic 2:3:4:6 ratio on a 2:3-proportioned page; Jan Tschichold popularized these constructions in the mid-1950s, though they are modern reconstructions of old book layouts, not proven historical recipes. For catalogs, flyers and screens, a canon wastes surface, so size margins from real constraints: binding eats the inner margin, bleeds change perceived width, barcodes and footers must fit, and thumbs cover the bottom. The key move: body-text leading becomes the grid unit - 10 pt type on 12 pt leading means a 12 pt (4.233 mm) baseline grid, and everything with height gets counted in whole lines so neighboring columns share a rhythm. Columns follow content: aim for 45-75 characters per line, about 66 in the comfortable middle; twelve narrow columns are a flexible division, not twelve text columns. Fields and gutters are whole numbers of lines, images occupy whole fields with edges locked to module boundaries, and you finish with a four-question check - hierarchy visible, smallest text legible on the target tech, measure right, elements returning to rhythm - then export as a DTP spec, 1:1 PDF, SVG or CSS Grid.
ptrs: Margins by canon: the Van de Graaf construction divides the page into ninths - inner margin 1/9 of the width, outer 2/9, top 1/9 of the height, bottom 2/9 - giving the classic 2:3:4:6 ratio on a 2:3-proportioned page; Tschichold popularized these constructions in the mid-1950s, though they are modern reconstructions, not proven historical recipes.

Margins by decision: for catalogs, flyers and screens a canon wastes surface, so size margins from real constraints - binding eats the inner margin, bleeds change perceived width, barcodes and footers must fit, thumbs cover the bottom.

The key move: body-text leading becomes the grid unit - 10 pt type on 12 pt leading means a 12 pt (4.233 mm) baseline grid, and everything with height (type area, modules, images, spacing) gets counted in whole lines so neighboring columns share a rhythm.
Columns follow content: aim for 45-75 characters per line (~66 is the comfortable middle); twelve narrow columns are a flexible division - text might span 3 or 4, images any number.

Modules and images: fields and gutters are whole numbers of lines (one-line gutters are classic); images occupy whole fields like 2x1 or 3x2, edges locked to module boundaries, so an image's bottom lands on a text baseline.
Finish with a four-question check (hierarchy visible? smallest text legible on target tech? measure right? elements returning to rhythm?) and export as a DTP spec, 1:1 PDF, SVG or CSS Grid.
items.why: Bro, your reel covers and carousels are a publication whether you named them one or not. A baseline grid is the difference between 'a collection of posts' and 'a brand'. Decide format, margins, leading and columns ONCE, and every thumbnail after that takes minutes and still lines up with the last forty. Consistency is what makes people trust the suit before they hear the pitch.
items.example: Apply it to an Instagram carousel: phone format, symmetric margins, pick one body size and leading, set four columns, place every image across exactly two of them and keep every caption one grid line tall. Swiped end to end, the slides line up like pages of one book instead of six separate flyers.

questions.q: How does the Van de Graaf construction divide the page?
questions.a: Into ninths: inner margin 1/9 of the width, outer 2/9, top 1/9 of the height, bottom 2/9.

questions.q: What becomes the base unit of the whole grid?
questions.a: The body text's leading (line height) - everything with height is counted in whole lines.

questions.q: What line length is recommended for running text?
questions.a: About 45 to 75 characters per line, with roughly 66 as the comfortable middle.

items.plain: A grid is an invisible ruler system under a page. The designer decides the margins and column lines once, then every photo, headline and paragraph must snap to those lines - like lining up furniture along floor tiles instead of shoving it anywhere. That is why some pages feel calm and tidy before you even read a word.

items.headline: Cross the Line, Lose the Room
items.deck: One invisible line between two characters decides whether your scene reads clearly or feels wrong. Keep the camera on one side and the room stays oriented; cross it and the audience's mental map flips.
items.lead: The 180 degree rule draws an imaginary axis between two characters - or a character and an object - and tells you to keep every camera setup on one side of it, so the left/right relationship on screen never flips. Follow it and the scene's geography stays readable; cross it and viewers feel disoriented - which is exactly why directors break it on purpose.
items.body: The 180 degree rule draws an imaginary axis between two characters - or a character and an object - and tells you to keep every camera setup on one side of it, so the left/right relationship on screen never flips. Follow it and the scene's geography stays readable; cross it and viewers feel disoriented - which is exactly why directors break it on purpose. Each choice says something: following the rule establishes orientation, breaking it signals unease, bending it signals a gradual change. Heat's restaurant scene is the textbook follow: the line runs across the table through Pacino and De Niro, Pacino keeps looking camera right and De Niro camera left, so the viewer never loses the room. With a crowd, treat the set like a stage play and keep your setups 'in the seats' on one side; in chases, a car moving right-to-left must hold that screen direction across cuts or it looks like it turned around - Dumb and Dumber holds it from Nebraska to Aspen. Breaking with intent works: in 25th Hour, Spike Lee has Ed Norton and the detective both look camera left during the drug bust, and the flipped geography puts you inside Norton's confusion; The Shining, Requiem for a Dream, Do the Right Thing, American Beauty and Hulk also cross deliberately. And you can bend the line legally: a neutral shot straight on the axis (Ocean's Eleven), camera movement that crosses during one unbroken take (the dolly around Neil in Heat), or a cutaway to something with no orientation (used for fight geography in Hero).
ptrs: What each choice says: following the rule establishes orientation, breaking it signals unease, bending it signals a gradual change in the scene.
Heat's restaurant scene is the textbook follow: the line runs across the table through Pacino and De Niro - Pacino keeps looking camera right, De Niro camera left, so the viewer never loses the room.

Groups and vehicles: with a crowd, treat the set like a stage play and keep your setups 'in the seats' on one side; in chases, a car moving right-to-left must hold that screen direction across cuts or it looks like it turned around (Dumb and Dumber holds it from Nebraska to Aspen).

Breaking with intent: in 25th Hour, Spike Lee has Ed Norton and the detective both look camera left during the drug bust - the flipped geography puts you inside Norton's confusion; The Shining, Requiem for a Dream, Do the Right Thing, American Beauty and Hulk also cross deliberately.

Bending resets the line legally: a neutral shot straight on the axis (Ocean's Eleven), camera movement that crosses during one unbroken take (the dolly around Neil in Heat), or a cutaway to something with no orientation (used for fight geography in Hero).
items.why: You shoot talking-head reels and two-person skits, so listen up: when an edit of two people talking feels 'weird' and you can't say why, nine times out of ten someone crossed the line. Put an imaginary rope between your subjects, keep the phone on one side, and your cuts snap together like Lego. Then, the day you WANT the audience squirming - that's when you cross it on purpose, like Spike Lee.
items.example: Shooting a two-person podcast clip: draw the axis between the speakers and put both camera angles on the same side of it - speaker A always faces screen-left, speaker B screen-right, and the edit stays readable. Want the moment an argument turns hostile to feel wrong in the stomach? That's the moment you earn a line cross.

questions.q: What is 'the line' in the 180 degree rule?
questions.a: An imaginary axis between two characters (or a character and an object); the camera stays on one side of it.

questions.q: What does deliberately crossing the line usually signal?
questions.a: Disorientation or unease - that something in the scene has gone wrong.

questions.q: Name one way to bend the rule without confusing viewers.
questions.a: A neutral shot on the axis, camera movement across it in one unbroken take, or a cutaway that resets orientation.

items.plain: Imagine two friends talking across a table while you watch from one side: the friend on your left stays on your left in every photo you take. If you walked to the other side of the table mid-conversation, they would suddenly swap sides in your photos, as if they teleported. Films keep the camera on one side of an invisible line so people never 'teleport' between cuts.

items.headline: Vibe-Coded Apps Left the Door Open
items.deck: Security researchers examined 159,041 apps built with Lovable and found thousands handing database records to anyone who asked - including 80,000 profiles, 200,000 chat messages and over 1,000 identity documents.
items.lead: German security firm Crissy Field, working with Handelsblatt, analyzed 159,041 projects built on the AI app-builder Lovable and found 24,664 sites that sent database records to visitors the moment the page loaded - no login, no interaction. With read-only requests they found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of those sites, plus passports, chat logs and payment data sitting in the open.
items.body: German security firm Crissy Field, working with Handelsblatt, analyzed 159,041 projects built on the AI app-builder Lovable and found 24,664 sites that sent database records to visitors the moment the page loaded - no login, no interaction. With read-only requests they found records containing email addresses in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of those sites, plus passports, chat logs and payment data sitting in the open. Using Common Crawl data, they identified projects from December 2025 to September 2026; 34,545 used the Supabase database service, which they focused on as the most widely used option - Lovable's newer built-in database was not examined. The worst cases: a German lifestyle forum exposed over 80,000 profiles (names, emails, birth dates, gender) plus more than 200,000 chat messages; a service provider exposed 1,000+ records with passport numbers, expiration dates and nationalities; another left 280,000 customer emails readable; event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of ticket and food-sale records including payment information. The researchers stress the 30% figure (7,403 of 24,664) is not a confirmed leak rate - email fields can be public contact data, email-free personal records get missed, and the Common Crawl sample isn't representative of all Lovable apps. The problem scales badly because Lovable's database integrations follow recurring patterns, so an access trick that works on one app often works on the next, while the platform's terms put responsibility for data handling on customers who may have no technical background. Their prescription: before an app touches real customer data, get access permissions, interfaces and account separation reviewed by an expert - automated checks are no substitute. Lovable was contacted through Handelsblatt before publication, and the researchers published no access details. The story drew 650+ points on Hacker News, where commenters debated whether blame sits with the platform's defaults or with users shipping without reviews - community reaction, not established fact.
ptrs: Method: using Common Crawl data they identified projects from December 2025 to September 2026; 34,545 used Supabase, the database service they focused on; Lovable's newer built-in database was not examined.

Worst cases: a German lifestyle forum exposed 80,000+ profiles (names, emails, birth dates, gender) plus 200,000+ chat messages; a service provider exposed 1,000+ records with passport numbers, expiration dates and nationalities; another left 280,000 customer emails readable; organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of sales records including payment info.

Honesty about the number: the researchers stress the 30% figure (7,403 of 24,664) is not a confirmed leak rate - email fields can be public contact data, email-free personal records get missed, and the Common Crawl sample isn't representative.

Why it scales badly: Lovable's database integrations follow recurring patterns, so an access trick that works on one app often works on the next - and the platform's terms put responsibility for data handling on customers, many with no technical background.

The fix they prescribe: before an app handles real customer data, get access permissions, interfaces and account separation reviewed by an expert - automated checks are no substitute; Lovable was contacted via Handelsblatt and no access details were published.
HN discussion (650+ points): commenters debated whether blame sits with the platform's defaults or with users shipping without security reviews - community reaction, not established fact.
items.why: Challenge accepted: you WILL build with AI app builders - everyone your age with ideas will. The transfer lesson works on any stack with row-level security (Supabase, Firebase, whatever ships next): the first question is always 'can an anonymous visitor read this table?' Vibe-coding gets you to demo day; a permission review is what gets you to real users without becoming a cautionary headline.
items.example: Test your own app like the researchers did: open your site logged-out, watch the database calls the page makes in dev tools, and replay them - if you can pull other people's rows without a session, your access rules are off. They needed nothing fancier than read-only requests to find passports.

questions.q: How many Lovable projects did the researchers examine?
questions.a: 159,041, identified through Common Crawl data (December 2025 - September 2026).

questions.q: What made the leaks easy to repeat across apps?
questions.a: Lovable's database integrations follow recurring patterns, so one access approach works against many apps.

questions.q: Is the 30% figure a confirmed leak rate?
questions.a: No - the researchers explicitly say it isn't: email fields can be public, email-free records get missed, and the sample isn't representative.

items.plain: Some websites store information in a filing cabinet that answers requests. A well-built site asks 'who is asking?' before handing anything over; these apps skipped that question, so anyone walking up could read the files. It is like a hotel where every room key opens every room.

items.headline: Italy's €805M Bill for Gallery Peeking
items.deck: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million ($887 million) for tapping Android users' photo and video galleries through a Facebook sharing feature without specific consent - around 20 million users in Italy affected.
items.lead: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million ($887 million) on Saturday after finding the company accessed Android users' photos and videos without obtaining consent or adequately informing them. The access came through a Facebook app feature that suggested content from users' personal galleries they might want to post.
items.body: Italy's data protection authority fined Meta €805 million ($887 million) on Saturday after finding the company accessed Android users' photos and videos without obtaining consent or adequately informing them. The access came through a Facebook app feature that suggested content from users' personal galleries they might want to post. Meta now has 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately; around 20 million Android users in Italy were affected. The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta's global revenue, per the authority, and the investigation began in 2025. Meta said it will appeal: a spokesperson called the fine 'disproportionate' and said users must grant device permission before the feature can operate and can change that permission anytime in settings. Notably, the investigation did not cover whether gallery content was used to train AI models - a practice Meta denied - and the authority reserved the right to separately assess a feature launched in 2026 that processes gallery content in the cloud.
ptrs: Meta has 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately; around 20 million Android users in Italy were affected.
The fine equals about 0.47% of Meta's global revenue, per the authority; the investigation began in 2025.
Meta will appeal: a spokesperson called the fine 'disproportionate' and said users must grant device permission before the feature works and can change it anytime in settings.

The investigation did not cover whether gallery content trained AI models - a practice Meta denied - and the authority reserved the right to assess a 2026 feature that processes gallery content in the cloud.
items.why: File this under 'rules your future apps live under': any app you build that touches the camera roll needs specific, informed consent - not implied, not buried. And watch the reserved part: cloud processing of personal galleries is the next fight, and that one is directly an AI story. The regulators are reading the same roadmap you are.
items.example: Building a meme-maker that reads the camera roll? This ruling hands you the checklist: ask consent for the exact use, keep the feature off by default, and treat 'process in the cloud' as a separate question from 'process on device' - because that is exactly how the regulator split it.

questions.q: How big is the fine and who issued it?
questions.a: €805 million (about $887 million), from Italy's data protection authority.

questions.q: What triggered the access?
questions.a: A Facebook app feature that suggested photos and videos from users' personal galleries to post.

questions.q: Did the ruling cover AI training on the photos?
questions.a: No - the authority said the investigation did not cover that; Meta denied the practice.

items.plain: Your phone's gallery is like a drawer of printed photos. The regulator says Facebook's app kept suggesting pictures from that drawer without clearly asking first. Italy fined the company and gave it 60 days to switch the feature off unless people explicitly say yes.

items.headline: Raise a Spark: Watch a Brain Learn
items.deck: An interactive article hands you a digital creature with a four-neuron brain and three sliders - wire it yourself, then watch an algorithm take it from stuck to expert in 2,000 tries.
items.lead: 'Watch a Brain Learn' by Aatish Bhatia and neuroscientist Arkarup Banerjee lets you wire a spark's tiny brain - two eye neurons, two flipper neurons, three numbers - and steer it toward light, then hands the job to a learning algorithm. After 50 tries it meanders, after 250 it (weirdly) avoids the light, after 500 it charges, and by 2,000 tries it is an expert that clings to the light and turns on a dime.
items.body: 'Watch a Brain Learn' by Aatish Bhatia and neuroscientist Arkarup Banerjee lets you wire a spark's tiny brain - two eye neurons, two flipper neurons, three numbers - and steer it toward light, then hands the job to a learning algorithm. After 50 tries it meanders, after 250 it (weirdly) avoids the light, after 500 it charges, and by 2,000 tries it is an expert that clings to the light and turns on a dime. Your task in the first interactive: tweak the three sliders (straight connection, crossed connection, drive) and get the score - average light encountered over 100 trials - above 0.5. The algorithm wiggles the wiring randomly before each trial; if the trial beats a running average of recent rewards, the wiring shifts toward the wiggle, otherwise away (reward = average brightness along the path, 500 time steps per trial). It is a version of REINFORCE from Ronald Williams, 1992, using weight perturbation; OpenAI used a similar idea, evolution strategies, in 2017 to play Atari. Watching hundreds of novice sparks trace jittery, non-straight paths through the space of possible brains, all converging on the same sweet spot, makes one thing visceral: learning isn't linear. Flip the reward and behavior flips - punished for seeking light, sparks learn to FLEE or FREEZE; rewarded for approaching at speed, they learn to FIGHT. The biology parallel: baby songbirds learn to sing by babbling random variations and getting dopamine bursts when a variation nears their memory of an adult's song - reinforcement with no teacher; your brain runs the same trick with about 86 billion neurons instead of 4.
ptrs: Your task in the first interactive: tweak the three sliders (straight connection, crossed connection, drive) and get the score - average light encountered over 100 trials - above 0.5.

The algorithm: before each trial the wiring wiggles randomly; if the trial beats a running average of recent rewards, the wiring shifts toward the wiggle, otherwise away (reward = average brightness along the path, 500 time steps per trial) - a version of REINFORCE (Ronald Williams, 1992) using weight perturbation; OpenAI used a similar idea, evolution strategies, in 2017 to play Atari.
Watch the paths: hundreds of novice sparks each trace jittery, non-straight routes through the space of possible brains - and all converge on the same sweet spot. Learning isn't linear.
Flip the reward and behavior flips: punished for seeking light, sparks learn to FLEE or FREEZE; rewarded for approaching at speed, they learn to FIGHT - same algorithm, different incentive.

Biology parallel: baby songbirds learn to sing by babbling random variations and getting dopamine bursts when a variation nears their memory of an adult's song - reinforcement with no teacher; your brain runs the same trick with ~86 billion neurons instead of 4.
items.why: RL is coming for you in the AIML syllabus, and reading policy-gradient equations cold is hard mode. Fifteen minutes FEELING reward shaping with sliders gives you the intuition the math later formalizes. When PPO and RLHF show up in class, you'll already know what a reward-hacked policy looks like - you watched a baby spark freeze in the dark because the incentive told it to.
items.example: Do it tonight on your phone: open the article, beat 0.5 by hand first and notice how long trial-and-error takes YOU. Then run the self-learning stage and watch the 250-try 'avoiding' phase - a wrong intermediate strategy that still improved on stuck. That phase is exactly what reward-shaping bugs look like in real RL projects.

questions.q: Which three numbers define the spark's brain wiring?
questions.a: The straight and crossed connection strengths, plus drive (speed when there is no light).

questions.q: How does the algorithm decide which way to shift the wiring?
questions.a: It compares each trial's reward to a running average: better shifts toward the random wiggle, worse shifts away.

questions.q: What happens when the reward is flipped to punish light-seeking?
questions.a: The same algorithm learns to flee or freeze instead - the incentive, not the code, picks the behavior.

items.plain: Teaching this creature works like training a puppy with treats: try something, get a treat when it works, a stern 'no' when it doesn't. The puppy doesn't understand your words - it just does more of whatever earned treats. That treat-feedback loop is reinforcement learning, and it is one way big AI models learn too.

items.headline: Don't build a better brain. Give it stairs
items.deck: After 600 experiments on LeCun-team's JEPA world model, one researcher found the model's predictions already match perfect physics - the wins came from planning tricks: subgoals every 25 steps took success from 22% to 80%, and a memory graph with priced jumps hit 85%.
items.lead: Haddy Alchaer ran 600 experiments on LeWM, a JEPA world model released this year by a team including Yann LeCun, and the headline result flips the usual instinct: swapping the model's learned predictions for the simulator's perfect physics changed success from 78% to... 77%. The model wasn't the bottleneck - the way it was used for planning was, and four training-free planning methods took long-horizon success from 22% to 85%.
items.body: Haddy Alchaer ran 600 experiments on LeWM, a JEPA world model released this year by a team including Yann LeCun, and the headline result flips the usual instinct: swapping the model's learned predictions for the simulator's perfect physics changed success from 78% to... 77%. The model wasn't the bottleneck - the way it was used for planning was, and four training-free planning methods took long-horizon success from 22% to 85%. JEPA - joint-embedding predictive architecture - is LeCun's answer to generative world models: instead of predicting the future in pixels, an encoder compresses each frame into an embedding, a predictor forecasts the next embedding given an action, and a planner tries hundreds of action sequences inside that embedding space, picking whichever ends closest to the goal's embedding. LeWM's benchmark is Push-T, where a robot pushes a T-shaped block to a target. The experiments: used as published, LeWM solves 22% of tasks with the goal 75 steps away, but 89.7% with the goal 25 steps away - its useful planning horizon is about 25 steps. So method one chains subgoals 25 steps apart: success jumps to 80%, while perfect physics all at once manages only 42%. Method two builds a memory graph from about 460,000 embedded demonstration states - embedding distance ranks a reachable subgoal as closer 87% of the time, so the graph doubles as a map of what's reachable. Free jumps between demonstrations let the planner cheat (318 of 1,015 plans strung 6+ jumps into physically impossible paths; 62% success); charging a cost per jump reached 85%, matching expert-provided subgoals. He also caught the standard benchmark being easier than it looks (84% of its goals already sit on demonstration flows; the official 50-episode score of 68% drops to 44% on 250 fresh episodes). Method three fills memory gaps with shifted, rotated and mirrored demonstration segments - deleting states near the goal crashed success from 93% to 32%, transforms restored it to 85%. And method four found the goal images accidentally included the robot pusher's own position: scoring block-only instead of block-plus-pusher flipped 30 of 50 hard tasks from failure to success, with zero flipping back - a split that happens by chance about twice in a billion.
ptrs: JEPA in one breath: encoder compresses each frame into an embedding, predictor forecasts the next embedding given an action, planner searches hundreds of action sequences in embedding space for the one ending nearest the goal - no pixel prediction needed.
The shocker: with expert subgoals, vanilla LeWM scores 78% vs 77% with the simulator's perfect physics swapped in - along trained paths, its predictions are already as good as reality for planning.

Method 1 - stairs, not leaps: LeWM solves 89.7% of 25-step goals but 22% of 75-step ones; chaining 25-step subgoals scores 80%, while perfect physics on the whole 75 steps gets 42%. Extra search (4x runs) added under a point.

Method 2 - a memory graph of ~460,000 embedded demonstration states; embedding distance identifies reachable subgoals 87% of the time; pricing each jump between demonstrations took success from 62% (with 318 of 1,015 plans abusing jumps) to 85%, matching expert subgoals.

Benchmark gotcha: 84% of standard-test goals sit on demonstration flows, and the official 68% score fell to 44% on 250 fresh episodes - changing only the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 outcomes.

Methods 3+4: fill memory gaps with shifted/rotated/mirrored segments (93% crashed to 32% with goal states deleted; transforms restore 85%); and score the goal by the block only, not the pusher - 30 of 50 hard tasks flipped from fail to success, 0 the other way.
items.why: Everyone's instinct is 'train a bigger model', bro - this guy got 4x better results by rearranging how the model THINKS at test time. When your projects hit a ceiling, check your scaffolding before your weights. It's the studious version of work smarter.
items.example: The 22-to-80 jump in one line: instead of asking the model to imagine all 75 steps to the goal in one shot (22% success), hand it a checkpoint every 25 steps - the distance where it already scores 89.7% - and let it climb three short stairs (80%). Same weights, zero retraining.

questions.q: What are JEPA's three parts?
questions.a: An encoder that turns each observation into a compact embedding, a predictor that forecasts the next embedding from the current one plus an action, and a planner that searches action sequences in embedding space for the one ending closest to the goal.

questions.q: Why did chaining 25-step subgoals beat perfect physics?
questions.a: LeWM's accurate planning horizon is about 25 steps (89.7% success there); chaining keeps every search inside that range, while even exact physics planning all 75 steps at once only reached 42%.

questions.q: What was wrong with the goal images in the hard test?
questions.a: They included the robot pusher's position, so the planner also tried to match where the pusher stood; scoring the block's position alone flipped 30 of 50 tasks from failure to success, with none flipping back.

items.plain: Imagine giving directions to a friend across town: naming every single turn from memory gets them lost, but giving them three landmarks to hit in order works. This research shows AI planners are the same - they're accurate over short stretches, so chaining short hops beats one heroic long guess, no extra training needed.

items.headline: A poster is decisions, not decorations
items.deck: The Poster Manual's anatomy lesson: order the information first, find a concept (not a texture), and let hierarchy, scale, spacing and tension do the work - a small red word can beat a big gray headline.
items.lead: The Poster Manual's Lesson 5 breaks a poster into the decisions that make it work: start by ordering what the viewer needs to know, find a concept that gives the visuals direction, then tune hierarchy, scale, spacing, balance and rhythm until every element relates. Great type, a beautiful image and nice colors can still make a weak poster - what matters is how they work together.
items.body: The Poster Manual's Lesson 5 breaks a poster into the decisions that make it work: start by ordering what the viewer needs to know, find a concept that gives the visuals direction, then tune hierarchy, scale, spacing, balance and rhythm until every element relates. Great type, a beautiful image and nice colors can still make a weak poster - what matters is how they work together. First, write the information down and rank it: a festival's headliner, date and ticket link don't deserve equal attention, and the message ('a concert is happening') is separate from the visual idea. Second, the concept: 'rock festival' isn't one - rusty grungy type is just texture. A concept is the central idea that connects what the poster is about with how you communicate it; a desert festival and an abandoned-factory one promise different things. Hierarchy is not just size: a small red word in a black-and-white poster can outrank a large gray headline, a face steals attention from type, and the real test is whether the viewer knows where to begin - then whether they can find the date. Scale works through comparison (huge word, tiny date), and contrast can come from weight, blur, geometry or density - pick one that serves the subject. Spacing tells us what belongs together: date under venue becomes a unit, and one name with extra air reads as the headliner before you change its size. Alignment connects across distance, which is why a tiny accidental offset feels unsettled - you almost established a relationship. Balance isn't centeredness (a large pale image can balance a small heavy type block), and tension lives in the 'almost': almost touching, almost aligned - sometimes useful discomfort, sometimes move it or commit. Type is seen before it's read; try one family and change size, weight, spacing, position before blaming the font. Give the image a role (subject, mood, idea, or something for type to answer to); let one accent color link date-venue-tickets; treat empty space as shapes in the composition; and use repetition to build rhythm, then decide where it stops.
ptrs: Order first: write down every piece of information and rank it - headliner, date, venue, ticket link don't deserve equal attention; keep the message separate from the visual idea.

Concept over texture: 'rock festival = grungy type' is a texture, not a concept - the concept is the central idea that connects subject and communication (desert festival vs abandoned factory promise different things).
Hierarchy is not size: a small red word can beat a large gray headline; a face steals attention; check what actually comes first, then whether the date and venue are findable next.
Scale and contrast work through comparison - exaggerate the difference while exploring; one well-chosen contrast (weight, blur, geometry, density) beats five random ones.
Spacing groups, alignment connects: date under venue reads as a unit; one name with extra air reads as headliner; a tiny accidental offset feels wrong because you 'almost' made a relationship.

The rest of the toolkit: balance without centering; tension in the 'almost' positions; type is seen before it's read (change size/weight/spacing before changing fonts); give the image a role; one accent color to link related info; empty space is a shape; repetition builds rhythm - decide where it stops.
items.why: Your thumbnails and TechBlast covers ARE posters, bro - 2 seconds of attention, one winner-takes-all glance. Rank your info, pick ONE concept, and let a single loud accent point at the tap. That's the whole suit.
items.example: The lesson's own hierarchy test: put a small red word next to a large gray headline and watch the red one win - proof that making your headline bigger doesn't guarantee it leads. Before resizing anything in your next cover, decide what should come first and check what actually does.

questions.q: What should you do before touching fonts or colors?
questions.a: Write down all the information the poster must carry and rank it - the ranking sets the hierarchy; and find the concept, the central idea connecting subject and communication.

questions.q: Why can a small red word beat a big gray headline?
questions.a: Hierarchy is created by contrast, not just size - color, isolation and imagery all direct attention, so a large low-contrast headline can lose to a small high-contrast element.

questions.q: Why does a tiny accidental offset feel unsettling in a layout?
questions.a: Alignment creates relationships across distance; an offset 'almost' establishes one and fails to follow through - and 'almost' positions read as unresolved unless used deliberately as tension.

items.plain: A poster is like telling one friend a secret at a noisy party: you lean in and say the most important thing first, not everything at the same volume. Designers do that with size, color and spacing - the biggest or brightest thing is what you 'hear' first, and everything else queues politely behind it.
items.image_alt: A poster frame where one tiny bright word shape outshines a huge dull gray headline block, with a face silhouette pulling a third arrow of attention.
items.info_alt: Diagram: an eye shape entering a poster frame, a numbered path - no, a bold arrow visiting a big shape first, then a small bright shape, then a quiet block of lines at the bottom.
items.info_caption: Attention has an order: the loudest element wins the first look - the bright small thing beats the big dull thing - supporting info queues last.

items.headline: Leave room for the nose
items.deck: Composition is how you arrange the shot: eyes a third down in closeups, never crop limbs at joints, space in the direction people look or move - and backgrounds that tell the story instead of growing out of heads.
items.lead: Tom Barrance's framing guide at Learn About Film teaches composition as arrangement: put things clearly off-center for a natural look, give people more space in the direction they're looking or moving, keep eyes about a third of the way down in closeups, and mind what the frame's edges and background are doing. Small arrangements, huge difference in how professional a shot feels.
items.body: Tom Barrance's framing guide at Learn About Film teaches composition as arrangement: put things clearly off-center for a natural look, give people more space in the direction they're looking or moving, keep eyes about a third of the way down in closeups, and mind what the frame's edges and background are doing. Small arrangements, huge difference in how professional a shot feels. The rule of thirds gets a sensible treatment: placing important things or edges about a third of the way across, up or down the screen works, and many cameras can overlay the grid - but judging whether the image looks right matters more than following a rigid rule. For closeups, eyes sit about a third of the way down; too low or too high just looks wrong. At the edges, don't crop people's arms or legs at the joints. The space a person looks or moves into is called looking space or nose room - leave more of it in front of the face than behind it, and when two people look at each other across a cut, their looking directions should line up (that's eyeline match). Going off-natural on purpose is a tool too: centered compositions look formal, sometimes odd; symmetry can look cool; a slanted camera (the Dutch angle) makes things strange or scary - but make the angle obvious or people read it as a mistake, and really unbalanced compositions make viewers uneasy. Finally, the background: avoid lines or objects growing out of people's heads (move until they're gone), blur confusing backgrounds with a longer lens if you can, accept that plain is better than confusing but boring - and ideally pick a background that tells us about the story, like the presenter standing in front of the very building he's discussing.
ptrs: Off-center = natural: place key things about a third across/up/down (cameras can overlay the grid) - but trust your eye over the rigid rule.
Closeups: eyes about a third of the way down the frame; too low or too high reads as wrong.
Edges: never crop arms or legs at the joints.
Looking space / nose room: more space in front of the face than behind it, in the direction of looking or moving; across a cut, two people's looking directions should line up (eyeline match).

Deliberate weirdness: centered = formal (sometimes odd), symmetry can look cool, Dutch angle = strange/scary - but make it obvious or it reads as a mistake; really unbalanced frames make viewers uneasy.
Backgrounds: nothing growing out of heads; blur or move confusing backgrounds; plain beats confusing but is boring; best is a background that tells the story.
items.why: Your reels are one person talking to a phone, bro - which means composition IS your production design. Eyes a third down, nose room, nothing sticking out of your head, and a background that says something. Instant 'wait, why does this look pro now'.
items.example: The guide's own before/after logic: a presenter filmed with the building he's discussing behind him beats the same presenter against a blank wall - plain is better than confusing, but a background that tells the story beats both. Same person, same camera, different arrangement.

questions.q: What is looking space (nose room)?
questions.a: Extra space left in the frame in the direction a person is looking or moving - more in front of the face than behind it.

questions.q: Where should the eyes sit in a closeup?
questions.a: About a third of the way down the frame; noticeably lower or higher reads as wrong.

questions.q: What's the background hierarchy?
questions.a: Best: a background that tells the story. Acceptable: plain. Avoid: confusing - and never let lines or objects grow out of people's heads.

items.plain: When you photograph a friend who's looking to the left, it feels right to leave more space on the left side, as if their gaze needs somewhere to land. Film composition is a handful of arrangements like that - where the eyes sit, where limbs get cropped, what's behind the person - that quietly make a shot feel natural or awkward.
items.image_alt: A paper face in profile looking right, with generous empty space ahead of the nose and a cramped sliver behind the head.
items.info_alt: Diagram: two frames side by side - one face squashed against the frame edge with a cross mark, one face with open space ahead of its gaze and a check mark.
items.info_caption: Wrong: gaze hits the frame edge - Right: space waits where the eyes are going. The face sits off-center, eyes a third down.

items.headline: $11.4M of Nvidia gear vanishes
items.deck: Six pallets of Nvidia hardware reportedly disappeared between Oakland and Fort Worth - picked up by a truck wearing a food company's logo, tracked through hours-long stops, then lost in San Bernardino County. Police confirm a grand-theft investigation.
items.lead: Six pallets of Nvidia computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million vanished during a shipment from Oakland to Fort Worth, FreightWaves reports - the truck, displaying a food transportation company's logo at pickup, made several hours-long stops before investigators lost its trail in Southern California. Oakland police confirm an ongoing grand theft investigation after a complaint filed September 13.
items.body: Six pallets of Nvidia computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million vanished during a shipment from Oakland to Fort Worth, FreightWaves reports - the truck, displaying a food transportation company's logo at pickup, made several hours-long stops before investigators lost its trail in Southern California. Oakland police confirm an ongoing grand theft investigation after a complaint filed September 13. The Mercer News-reported details: the vehicle was collected in Oakland on August 29 for delivery to Fort Worth, then traveled south with extended stops before the trail went cold in San Bernardino County. Police caveats matter: the September 13 complaint date doesn't establish when the theft occurred, and police have not confirmed the $11.4 million valuation, the specific merchandise, or identified the cargo's owner, shipper, carrier or driver; no arrests, no recovery announced, and Nvidia hadn't responded to FreightWaves' requests for comment. The disappearance lands amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data-center freight involving other high-value tech shipments, and a separate $12 million cargo-theft investigation in which suspects allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight - authorities haven't linked the two. It's also not the region's first: during 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in Nvidia products, and in a separate September incident thieves stole two PlusAI trailers (one Nvidia-branded) from a Fremont warehouse - which turned out to contain roughly 40,000 pounds of sand; both were recovered nearby. On Hacker News the story drew ~290 points, with commenters trading cargo-fraud lore about fictitious pickups - community color, not verified fact.
ptrs: The report: six pallets of Nvidia hardware, a reported $11.4M, collected in Oakland Aug 29 for Fort Worth - gone; the truck showed a food-transport logo at pickup and was lost in San Bernardino County after several hours-long stops (FreightWaves, citing The Mercury News).

Police status: Oakland PD confirms a grand-theft investigation (complaint filed Sept 13) - but has NOT confirmed the valuation, the merchandise, or the owner/shipper/carrier/driver; no arrests or recovery announced.

The pattern: the case lands amid reports of ~$111M in stolen data-center freight, and a separate $12M cargo-theft probe involving suspects allegedly exploiting established trucking identities - not officially linked.

The prequels: $7.5M+ in Nvidia-product burglaries investigated in Fremont and Union City in 2025; and the thieves who stole two PlusAI trailers from Fremont got ~40,000 lbs of sand instead of GPUs (recovered).
HN colour: ~290 points; commenters swapped fictitious-pickup and cargo-fraud stories - discussion, not verified fact.
items.why: GPUs are officially the new gold bars, bro - trucks full of them are getting the heist-movie treatment. When you wonder why your RTX upgrade or cloud credits cost what they do, remember: the chips are valuable enough to steal by the pallet.
items.example: The alleged playbook, per the report: show up at the warehouse looking like a legitimate carrier (a food company's logo), collect the freight in broad daylight, then take the scenic route south with long stops until the trail goes cold. Carrier verification is exactly what FreightWaves' analysis says has to improve.

questions.q: What has police actually confirmed?
questions.a: That it's investigating a grand theft in East Oakland reported September 13. It has not confirmed the $11.4M valuation, the specific merchandise, the owner/shipper/carrier/driver, or made arrests.

questions.q: How was the shipment reportedly taken?
questions.a: A truck displaying a food transportation company's logo collected the pallets in Oakland for delivery to Fort Worth, then made extended stops heading south before investigators lost it in San Bernardino County.

questions.q: Is this an isolated incident?
questions.a: No - it lands amid reports of nearly $111M in stolen data-center freight, a separate $12M cargo-theft probe (not linked), and $7.5M+ in Nvidia-product burglaries investigated in Fremont and Union City in 2025.

items.plain: Computer chips for AI are now so valuable that a whole truckload can be worth over eleven million dollars - so one reportedly got stolen like in a heist movie: a truck pretending to be a food delivery picked up the pallets and simply never arrived. Police are investigating, but many details are still unconfirmed.
items.image_alt: A paper delivery truck with a peeled-off logo patch, six stacked pallets falling off its open back onto a winding road that fades into nothing.

items.headline: Decider: the model that just votes
items.deck: Perplexity's Decider v1.3 is an open Apache-licensed 'decision model': instead of generating text, it answers yes/no, multiple-choice and score questions with probabilities - for judging, routing, moderation and reranking - in a single forward pass.
items.lead: Perplexity released Decider v1.3 and the smaller distilled Decider Flash v1.3, both under the Apache license on Hugging Face, OpenRouter and its Decisions API. Decider is a 'decision model': give it an input plus questions with possible answers, and it returns a probability distribution over each question's answers - no token-by-token generation.
items.body: Perplexity released Decider v1.3 and the smaller distilled Decider Flash v1.3, both under the Apache license on Hugging Face, OpenRouter and its Decisions API. Decider is a 'decision model': give it an input plus questions with possible answers, and it returns a probability distribution over each question's answers - no token-by-token generation. It handles three question types - yes/no, multiple choice with custom labels, and ordered scores - and it's inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI's System One Model. The target jobs are the unglamorous workhorses usually forced through LLMs: judging outputs for faithfulness, quality and safety; routing requests to smaller or larger models by difficulty; moderation and security (including detecting prompt injection in tool outputs); filtering and tagging big collections; and retrieval reranking. The trick is structural: a request is one shared context (the state) plus many question blocks, each answer option pre-assigned a label token like A, B or C; a special marker token indicates where to read out the prediction, and at that position a learned linear 'decision head' maps the hidden state to per-option scores turned into probabilities. Multiple questions about the same input get answered in a single forward pass, sharing the computation - and because it learned a shared question-answering format across diverse tasks, it can take on new tasks through plain natural-language prompts, sitting between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. The v1.3 pair improves robustness across text and vision tasks via bidirectional attention, better-curated training data and a refined recipe, and adds 'locate', which highlights the selected content for named-entity recognition, personal-information identification and extractive question answering. Perplexity says it uses Decider internally and documented training and evaluation in the release post.
ptrs: What shipped: Decider v1.3 plus the smaller distilled Decider Flash v1.3 - Apache-licensed on Hugging Face, also via OpenRouter and the Perplexity Decisions API (Nov 12).

What a decision model is: a general-purpose classifier - input + questions with answer options in, probability distribution over each question's answers out; three question types: yes/no, multiple choice, ordered score.

What it's for: judging outputs (faithfulness, quality, safety), routing by difficulty, moderation and security (including prompt-injection detection in tool outputs), filtering/tagging, retrieval reranking.

How it works: one shared context plus question blocks with label tokens (A, B, C); a marker token marks where to read the prediction; a learned linear 'decision head' maps that hidden state to per-option probabilities - many questions, one forward pass.

Why it matters vs LLMs: tasks that never needed free-form text get probabilities without token-by-token generation, sharing compute across questions; unlike narrow classifiers it still takes new tasks via natural-language prompts. Inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI's System One Model.
v1.3 upgrades: bidirectional attention, better-curated data, refined recipe, text + vision robustness, and 'locate' - highlighting selected content for NER, PII detection and extractive QA.
items.why: Half the things people burn LLM tokens on are really just multiple-choice questions, bro - is this summary faithful, is this email phishing, which model should handle this. An open model that just VOTES with probabilities is cheaper, faster, and you can download it tonight.
items.example: The post's own shape: hand Decider a document and its summary as one shared context, then ask two questions in the same request - 'is the summary faithful?' and 'is it aimed at experts or a general audience?' - and get both probability answers from a single forward pass instead of two LLM calls.

questions.q: How is a decision model different from a chatbot?
questions.a: It doesn't generate text token by token; you give it an input plus questions with predefined answer options, and it returns a probability distribution over the answers via a learned decision head.

questions.q: What can it be used for?
questions.a: Judging outputs (faithfulness, quality, safety), routing requests to smaller or larger models, moderation and security like prompt-injection detection, filtering and tagging, and retrieval reranking.

questions.q: Can you actually get it?
questions.a: Yes - Decider v1.3 and the smaller distilled Flash v1.3 are Apache-licensed on Hugging Face, and also available through OpenRouter and Perplexity's Decisions API.

items.plain: Imagine asking a friend ten yes-or-no questions about one photo, and they answer all ten in one glance instead of describing the photo ten separate times. Decider works like that friend: it doesn't write essays - it just looks once and votes, with confidence percentages, which is exactly what filters and routers need.
items.image_alt: A paper ballot box shaped like a brain, with three question cards sliding in and three percentage-bar cards sliding out.
items.info_alt: Diagram: one shared document card feeds three question cards stacked together; a single arrow passes through one model box; three probability bars come out.
items.info_caption: One shared context + many question blocks - one forward pass through the decision head - probabilities out for every question at once.

items.headline: Man in the middle of your own fan
items.deck: A developer reverse-engineered his Coway air purifier to ditch its cloud: a Raspberry Pi as a Wi-Fi access point, mitmproxy reading the traffic, and an LLM doing the setup in minutes. The same toolkit shows what any device you own is phoning home.
items.lead: Scott J. got tired of his Coway air purifier's cloud app and reverse-engineered it: he put a Raspberry Pi between the fan and the internet as a Wi-Fi access point, redirected its traffic through mitmproxy, and read exactly what the device sends home - with an LLM doing the network setup unattended in minutes. The full write-up is a 680-point Hacker News hit.
items.body: Scott J. got tired of his Coway air purifier's cloud app and reverse-engineered it: he put a Raspberry Pi between the fan and the internet as a Wi-Fi access point, redirected its traffic through mitmproxy, and read exactly what the device sends home - with an LLM doing the network setup unattended in minutes. The full write-up is a 680-point Hacker News hit. His goal was domestic, not adversarial: tie the fan into his Apple Home 'Good Night' button so one tap kills the lights and cranks the white-noise fan. The blocker was the fan's encrypted chatter with Coway's IoCare cloud. Two things made the attempt timely: a recent security incident (October 2026) where the certificate authority eMudhra was found to have used very weak parameters for some private keys - meaning anyone could potentially mint trusted certificates for a while - and AI, because an LLM could configure the whole man-in-the-middle environment for him. He notes, with screenshots, that Claude declined the setup request under its cyber policy while ChatGPT obliged - his account, worth reading as one data point on how assistants treat dual-use networking help. The rig: a Raspberry Pi running its own isolated Wi-Fi network for the fan, nftables rules redirecting ports 80 and 443 into mitmproxy (which decrypts and logs the traffic), and - because the Pi's tiny antenna couldn't reach both the fan and his router - his laptop bridging the Pi to the home network over Ethernet. Once you sit between a device and the internet, he writes, you can see how it communicates - the first step to making it talk to you instead of the cloud. You can try the polite version tonight on your own gear: mitmproxy is free and open-source, and pointing your own phone at it reveals what your apps send, to whom, and how often.
ptrs: The project: liberate a Coway Airmega from its cloud so an Apple Home 'Good Night' button can kill the lights and crank the fan's white noise - 680 HN points.

The rig: Raspberry Pi as an isolated Wi-Fi access point for the fan; nftables redirecting ports 80/443 into mitmproxy to decrypt and log traffic; laptop bridging the Pi to the home network (the Pi's PCB antenna was too weak to span both rooms).
The timing: an October 2026 incident where CA eMudhra used very weak parameters for some private keys (potentially forgeable trusted certs) - plus LLMs making the whole MitM setup a minutes-long job.
The colour (his account, with screenshots): Claude declined the setup request under its cyber policy; ChatGPT obliged - one data point on how assistants treat dual-use help.
The lesson: sit between a device and the internet and you can see how it communicates - the first step to making it talk to you instead of the cloud.
Tonight's version: mitmproxy is free and open-source; proxy your OWN phone through it and watch what one app sends home - domains, frequency, payloads you can read.
items.why: This is the hacker version of 'you can just do things', bro: a Raspberry Pi, free software, and an LLM intern, and suddenly a 'locked' cloud gadget answers to HIM. Try the baby step - proxy your own phone tonight and read what one chatty app whispers home. You'll never look at 'free apps' the same.
items.example: His concrete chain, replicable on your own devices: device - Pi access point - nftables redirect of ports 80/443 - mitmproxy logs everything. Yours: install mitmproxy on your PC, set your phone's Wi-Fi proxy to the PC's IP and port 8080, install mitmproxy's certificate on the phone, open one app, and read its requests in the mitmproxy web UI. Own devices only.

questions.q: What does a man-in-the-middle setup show you?
questions.a: Everything a device sends and receives - by sitting between it and the internet you can read its traffic and learn its protocol, the first step to controlling it yourself instead of via the vendor's cloud.

questions.q: Why did he need a Raspberry Pi AND his laptop?
questions.a: The Pi ran its own isolated Wi-Fi network for the fan, but its small PCB antenna couldn't reach both the fan and the home router - so the laptop bridged the Pi to the home network over Ethernet.

questions.q: Is this legal to try?
questions.a: On your own devices, inspecting your own traffic with a tool like mitmproxy is a normal security-research exercise - intercepting other people's traffic or networks is not.

items.plain: Every smart gadget sends little letters home over the internet, and usually you can't read them because they're sealed. This is like making the gadget hand its letters to your own mailbox first: you open them, learn what it says, and eventually answer in the cloud's place - on gadgets you own, that's a fair and famous hobby.
items.image_alt: A paper air purifier whispering dotted letters into a tiny Raspberry Pi mailbox held open by a magnifying glass, the cloud above crossed with a slash.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a fan shape, arrow into a small computer box with an eye symbol, arrow onward to a crossed-out cloud, and a branch arrow down to a phone reading the logs.
items.info_caption: Fan - Pi access point + mitmproxy reads the traffic - cloud optional; the owner watches everything from their own screen.

items.headline: A 16B model on 1 GB of RAM
items.deck: The smolmaxxing project runs 16-billion-parameter models on a TV box and a 2013 iPad - with custom 1-bit kernels, a vocabulary diet, and a trick that pages model 'experts' from flash like a books-on-demand library.
items.lead: smolmaxxing is an open-source project with one mission: run the biggest language model possible on the smallest hardware you own. Its patched version of llama.cpp runs a 16B-parameter mixture-of-experts model on a Xiaomi TV box with 1.9 GB of RAM at 5.1 tokens per second - and even on a 2013 iPad Air with 1 GB of RAM.
items.body: smolmaxxing is an open-source project with one mission: run the biggest language model possible on the smallest hardware you own. Its patched version of llama.cpp runs a 16B-parameter mixture-of-experts model on a Xiaomi TV box with 1.9 GB of RAM at 5.1 tokens per second - and even on a 2013 iPad Air with 1 GB of RAM. The scoreboard is absurd: the TV box (an Amlogic chip with about 1 GB of usable RAM, Android 14, no root) runs Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tokens/s as its everyday model, and the jailbroken iPad (an Apple A7 from 2013, about 700 MB usable) runs a 1-bit 1.7B model at 24-26 tokens/s. Four techniques do the heavy lifting. First, kernels built for each chip: a 1-bit lookup-table kernel, plus repacked 2-bit and ternary formats for the TV's Cortex-A55, and special versions for the iPad's A7, which lacks dot-product instructions. Second, a vocabulary diet: most of a small model's vocabulary is rarely used, so those output rows get dropped - and on the TV a 'headless' mode kills the launcher and Google services while a model runs. Third, the star move: mixture-of-experts models only use a few 'expert' sub-networks per token, so the popular experts stay in RAM while the rest are read from flash on demand, with the next layer's experts prefetched - that is how 8B and 16B models run on 1 GB. Fourth, dense models bigger than RAM get streamed from flash at full speed. The catches are honest: you need their patched llama.cpp (stock builds can't load the repacked models), the iPad must be jailbroken, and every number is measured on the device itself across a 160-experiment public lab notebook, failures included.
ptrs: The project: smolmaxxing (MIT license) - a patch on llama.cpp that runs the biggest LLM a device can truly handle; every number measured on the device itself.

Scoreboard: Xiaomi TV Box S (1.9 GB RAM, ~1 GB usable, Android 14, no root) runs Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s daily and a 16B MoE model at 5.1 tok/s; a 2013 iPad Air (1 GB RAM, ~700 MB usable, jailbroken) runs a 1-bit 1.7B model at 24-26 tok/s and the same 16B at 2.6-4.5 tok/s.
Technique 1 - kernels per chip: a 1-bit lookup-table kernel plus repacked 2-bit and ternary formats, with special builds for chips lacking dot-product instructions.
Technique 2 - shrink the model's footprint: drop rarely-used vocabulary output rows; on the TV, 'headless' mode stops the launcher and Google services while the model runs.

Technique 3 - page experts from flash: MoE models use only a few experts per token, so hot experts live in RAM and cold ones stream from flash on demand, prefetched a layer ahead - the key to 16B on 1 GB.
Technique 4 - stream dense models bigger than RAM at the flash's full speed.
Catches: the repacked models need the patched llama.cpp (stock can't load them); the iPad path needs a jailbreak; the repo's EXPERIMENT.md logs all 160 experiments, failures included.
items.why: You keep thinking local AI needs a monster rig, bro - these folks ran a 16B model on a TV box. Your 16GB PC is a supercomputer by their standards, and the same tricks (quantized small models, llama.cpp) are exactly how you squeeze it. Legendary constraint-hacking.
items.example: The repo's own receipt: on the TV box, keeping only the popular experts in RAM and paging the rest from flash is what lets the 16B Ling-mini-2.0 model generate at 5.1 tokens/s in about 1 GB of usable memory - and the same box plays Qwen3.5-2B at 7.7 tok/s as the daily driver.

questions.q: How can a 16B model fit in 1 GB of RAM?
questions.a: It's a mixture-of-experts model: only a few expert sub-networks fire per token, so the popular experts stay in RAM and the rest are read from flash on demand, with the next layer's prefetched.

questions.q: What two tricks shrink a small model's RAM use further?
questions.a: Dropping rarely-used vocabulary output rows, and on the TV a 'headless' mode that stops the launcher and Google services while the model runs.

questions.q: Can you load these models in stock llama.cpp?
questions.a: No - the repacked 1-bit, 2-bit and ternary formats need the project's patched llama.cpp.

items.plain: Big AI models are like huge libraries that normally need a mansion. This project keeps only the most-used books in the house and sends a super-fast runner to the warehouse for the rest, right when each is needed. That's how a TV box with the memory of a budget phone can 'think' with a giant model.
items.image_alt: A tiny paper TV set and an old tablet, each with a giant brain-shaped cloud compressed into it by a paper press.
items.info_alt: Diagram: a small RAM box holding two glowing expert blocks; arrows stream more expert blocks from a large flash-storage box below, one arrow prefetches ahead.
items.info_caption: Hot experts stay in RAM - cold experts stream from flash on demand - the next layer's experts are prefetched before they're needed.

items.headline: 60-30-10: the color budget
items.deck: Designer Stefano Peschiera's rule: give 60% of your layout to a neutral main color, 30% to a contrasting secondary, and 10% to the loudest accent you own - reserved for the buttons that matter.
items.lead: The 60-30-10 rule budgets color like money: your main color covers 60% of the design, a secondary color takes 30%, and an accent gets just 10%. In the Dribbble design blog's guide, designer Stefano Peschiera shares the workflow he built around it - and why the smallest slice should be the most vibrant.
items.body: The 60-30-10 rule budgets color like money: your main color covers 60% of the design, a secondary color takes 30%, and an accent gets just 10%. In the Dribbble design blog's guide, designer Stefano Peschiera shares the workflow he built around it - and why the smallest slice should be the most vibrant. The roles are strict: the 60% main color should be a neutral that's easy on the eyes, the 30% secondary should contrast nicely with the main to create visual interest, and the 10% accent should be the most vibrant of the three, because its job is to emphasize critical items like call-to-action buttons. Distributing colors in these proportions visually organizes the design and adds balance. His palette-hunting trick: browse nature photos on Unsplash and extract three main colors that already match the ratio, taking the most vibrant as the accent - mother nature is the best designer to steal from. His process trick: wireframe in grayscale first - spacing and layout before color, with gray tones keeping the wireframe from looking dead - then apply the palette and iterate. And his favorite color-theory trick: stay away from pure grayscale and pure black, because pure grays barely exist in real life; always add a bit of saturation so colors feel natural and familiar.
ptrs: The budget: 60% main color, 30% secondary, 10% accent - the proportions visually organize and balance a design.
Casting: main = neutral, easy on the eyes; secondary = contrasts with the main for visual interest; accent = the most vibrant, saved for critical items like call-to-action buttons.
Palette hunting: extract three colors matching the ratio from nature photos (his source: Unsplash); the most vibrant becomes the accent.
Process: wireframe in grayscale first - spacing and layout before color - then apply the palette and iterate.
Bonus rule: avoid pure gray and pure black - they barely exist in real life; add a little saturation so colors feel natural.
items.why: Your reel covers and thumbnails need this, bro: pick a chill background (60), a supporting color (30), and let ONE loud color (10) scream 'tap here'. It's the difference between a designed post and a sticker explosion.
items.example: Peschiera's own workflow: pull three colors off a nature photo that already follows 60-30-10, wireframe the whole page in grays first, then pour the palette on - vibrant color lands only on the call-to-action, which is exactly why people click it.

questions.q: Which color gets only 10% - and why?
questions.a: The accent: it's the most vibrant of the three and its job is emphasizing critical items like call-to-action buttons, so a small dose keeps it loud.

questions.q: What kind of color should own the 60%?
questions.a: A neutral that's easy on the eyes - it covers most of the design, so it must never tire the viewer.

questions.q: Why design in grayscale first?
questions.a: It forces spacing and layout decisions before color, a constraint Peschiera calls productive - the palette is applied and iterated afterwards.

items.plain: Think of an outfit: mostly one calm color (your suit), a second color for support (your shirt), and one small loud piece (a bright tie). Websites work the same way - 60% calm, 30% support, 10% loud - and the loud 10% is where the 'buy' button lives.
items.image_caption: A 10x10 waffle of the color budget: 60 cells main (neutral) - 30 cells secondary - 10 cells accent (the loud one)
items.image_alt: A 10 by 10 waffle grid: sixty quiet cells, thirty contrasting cells, ten loud accent cells in one corner.

items.headline: Three lamps run Hollywood
items.deck: Key, fill, backlight - the three-point setup is so standard in narrative cinema it's virtually a rule. Learn what each lamp does, then break the ratio on purpose for comedy-bright or noir-dark moods.
items.lead: Three-point lighting is the default grammar of filming a person: a key light provides the main illumination, a fill light softens the shadows it creates, and a backlight separates the subject from the background. Film scholar Paul Ramaeker's explainer in The Conversation shows how this convention - and the ratio between its lamps - quietly writes the mood of everything from musicals to noir.
items.body: Three-point lighting is the default grammar of filming a person: a key light provides the main illumination, a fill light softens the shadows it creates, and a backlight separates the subject from the background. Film scholar Paul Ramaeker's explainer in The Conversation shows how this convention - and the ratio between its lamps - quietly writes the mood of everything from musicals to noir. The setup is so prevalent in narrative cinema that it's virtually a rule, often supplemented by a small eye-light to heighten an actor's expression; its most stylised form, glamour lighting, turned Marlene Dietrich into an icon in Josef von Sternberg's films. Then there's practical lighting: sources that seem to come from inside the story-world - a visible lamp, a window, the neon-soaked streets of Blade Runner - which cinematographers also use to pour colour into a scene with gels. The mood knob is the fill-to-key ratio. High-key lighting (lots of fill, low contrast, even brightness) dominated 1930s comedies and musicals; low-key lighting (little fill, hard light, deep defined shadows) belonged to horror and crime, and became the soul of film noir - mystery and moral darkness through concealment. A Cornell study found light levels in film have markedly declined since 1935: early arc lights were so brutal their ultraviolet radiation gave actors 'Klieg eyes', and as film stock and digital sensors grew more sensitive, sets could go darker - kinder to actors, richer for mood. Cinematographer James Wong Howe saw it coming in 1931: lighting had stopped meaning 'enough light to shoot' and become 'a visual, emotional foundation' for the film.
ptrs: The three points: key light = main illumination; fill light = fills in shadows on face and background; backlight = separates subject from the backdrop (less critical in colour).
The extras: an eye-light to heighten expressions; 'glamour lighting' (think Dietrich in von Sternberg's films) built for star iconography.
Practical lighting: light that seems to come from inside the scene - a lamp, a window, Blade Runner's neon - often with coloured gels bathing the frame.
The mood knob: high-key = high fill-to-key ratio, low contrast, even brightness (1930s comedies and musicals); low-key = low fill-to-key, hard light, deep shadows (horror, crime, film noir).
The trend: a Cornell study found film light levels have markedly declined since 1935 - sensitive stocks and sensors let sets go darker, sparing actors the UV-burn 'Klieg eyes' of early arc lights.
The mission statement (James Wong Howe, 1931): lighting went from 'enough light to permit photography' to 'a visual, emotional foundation'.
items.why: You shoot reels, bro, and this is the oldest cheat code in the game: one main lamp, one shadow-softener, one behind you. Nail that triangle and your bedroom looks like a studio; then starve the fill for instant drama.
items.example: Tonight's test: face a window (key), bounce a phone flashlight off a wall onto your shadow side (fill), and put a desk lamp behind your shoulder (backlight). Then switch the fill off - same face, same room, and it suddenly reads as a crime film. That's the fill-to-key ratio doing the storytelling.

questions.q: What does each of the three lights do?
questions.a: Key provides the main illumination, fill fills in the shadows on face and background, and backlight separates the subject from the backdrop.

questions.q: High-key vs low-key?
questions.a: The fill-to-key ratio: high-key means lots of fill - low-contrast, even brightness (comedies, musicals); low-key means little fill - hard light and deep shadows (horror, noir).

questions.q: What is practical lighting?
questions.a: Light that appears to come from sources inside the story-world - a visible lamp, a window, neon signs - often used with coloured gels to bathe a scene in colour.

items.plain: Imagine photographing a friend with one flashlight: half their face goes black. Add a second, weaker light on the dark side and the shadows soften. Put a third behind them and they pop off the background. Movies are lit exactly like that - and how strong light two is decides if it feels like a comedy or a horror film.
